item.title: You Will Listen to Carl on Dwarkesh
item.description: Again, if necessary
item.content:encoded:
Dwarkesh Podcast is steadily taking over the intellectual world, but his best episode languishes in obscurity. 68 thousand views? Only 25k for part 2?! War stories lady has 16 million! I’m of course referring to Dwarkesh’s 2023 interview with Carl Shulman.1 I believe it is the single most comprehensive and accessible exploration of AI risk and transformative AI that has ever been published.

Dwarkesh himself said that this episode made a bigger contribution to his world model than any other.2 Here I’ll explain why this episode is so valuable, but I’ll also be posting clips from it on Twitter with some commentary in the coming days, to drive the message home for those who need to hear it. I regard this as critical, under-maintained infrastructure for the AI discourse and I invite you to join me in trying to build it.

Why you need to watch this

The episode starts with a simple question, roughly: “can you describe the general dynamics and feedback loops involved with creating human-level artificial intelligence?” Do you have a coherent and compelling response to this question? Try it. I suspect a lot of people who buy the AGI/TAI hypothesis will leap to “well, assume a superintelligence. Wouldn’t it be able to do all kinds of wild things?” When challenged to explain why superintelligence is possible at all, you might add “well the AI companies are investing enormous resources into this, and scaling them up like crazy at the same time all these benchmarks are falling.”

Respectfully, everyone knows about the benchmarks and resources. They just disagree that we’re on a never-ending trajectory that arrives at superintelligence soon. They’ve seen other technologies grow quickly and every single one of them has stopped short of taking over the world. They expect the same here. The crux is about what conceptual framework we use to interpret the benchmarks and resources.

Sometimes, AGI/TAI believers will analogize to evolution and point to the human brain as an existence proof of general intelligence. They point out that the computational scale of AI training runs is approaching the total computation used in the brain, and that this means we’re nearing a particularly plausible period in which all human abilities might be eclipsed by faster and vastly more replicable AIs.

I’m on board with this, but Carl brings the receipts. He knows the numbers; he understands the conditions that led to the evolution of the brain and to what extent those conditions apply to other species, and all the costs and benefits involved. He also knows AI, from the hardware, to the industry, to the finance, to the applications. He explains how these things interact and tells a clear story of how we get from here to there.

Beyond just getting to impressive capabilities, Carl goes a step further, getting into the psychology and incentives of individual AIs and the implications this has for safety and alignment. The bit about wireheading is especially compelling. One of the evolutionary analogies you’ve heard suggests humans’ use of contraceptives is reason to be worried about alignment. There’s a more general principle underneath this analogy though: intelligence begets misalignment. Once a system understands its own drives and can predict how its actions will affect its own future behaviors, you’ve introduced an important discontinuity in training where even within-distribution tasks get reinterpreted in light of these meta-considerations. Understanding your own nature implies opportunities to change your nature that were theoretically present all along, but never acted on (or reinforced one way or another) because the agent wasn’t even smart enough to see the option. Once it can see the option, any desirable behavior learned before that point is a mere instinct that reason can attempt to override.

Then he hits you with part two

Going beyond the incentives and psychology of models and the companies that build them, Carl then does some global analysis about how misaligned AI might take over. I’ve been disappointed with many other takeover scenarios because they assume away all the hard parts. Carl presents the most compelling kind of takeover story: what I call the ‘minimum viable’ takeover. Rather than gesturing blindly at “abilities we can’t imagine” or “invents flawless new technology sufficient to achieve takeover,” Carl explains the very tangible steps a not-inscrutably-alien AI could take to gain familiar levels of power and influence and gradually scale up from there. I agree superintelligences are possible and can probably do more than this, but it is compelling to have a story all of whose steps make sense and none of which require big leaps or assumptions about what AI can or will do.

Thinking in the limit

I like this discussion so much because it’s a great example of thinking in the limit. Carl doesn’t just say “well the brain is a general intelligence, maybe AI can be too.” He explains the dynamic environment that generated (and limited) human brains and then thinks through how its contours will or won’t apply to AIs given what we know. He asks the right questions about how far the relevant constraints can be stretched and concludes that it’s reasonably likely AIs could supersede humans.

This is how to forecast the future:

  1. Know a lot about what’s going on presently

  2. Understand the dynamics of how things unfolded in the past

  3. Think of how those dynamics will manifest given what you know about our present situation

Carl does these as comprehensively as anyone in his discussion with Dwarkesh.

The limit of analogical reasoning

I think the type of reasoning above is truly the best you can do when it comes to forecasting unprecedented events. The best you can do can still be bad. These are still analogies we’re dealing with. Analogies can be better or worse, but they can never provide as much confidence as a logical proof based on stipulated or well-established facts. Still, if you’re not a (pejorative) frequentist, analogies of some kind are all you have. Name your reference class, describe how it applies, remain uncertain, but act on the possibilities that would be most important after you discount for how uncertain you are.

That’s the situation I think we’re in, but you need to listen to Carl first so you can decide for yourself.

1

Also available on all podcast apps.

2

He said this on the episode itself, which was 2.5 years ago now, but I have listened to everything he has published since and he has not made this claim for any other episode!

item.title: 12 Theses on Politics
item.description: We're all living in America
item.content:encoded:
I’m not emailing this one out because it’s neither my area of expertise (oops, see #7), nor one that I expect people to widely appreciate for reasons other than how good the takes are.1 That said, if you stumbled upon these, you’re free to let me know what you want to hear more about:

  1. Democrats should flood the conservative media zone. Get top Dems and Dem influencers on Rogan, Tucker, Megyn Kelly, Candace; do Fox News and even OAN/Newsmax interviews. The idea is that it’s much harder to say wildly untrue things about someone when they’re sitting right in front of you. If you keep your cool the host loses their edge and you stop being the farmode boogeyman for the audience. I think Sam Altman did a really good job on Tucker for example. Tucker accused him of murder to his face and he reacted pretty calmly, putting Tucker on the back foot. I don’t think Tucker’s audience came away thinking Altman was evil. There’s a risk that supply of partisan content is extremely elastic and new echo chambers pop up, but if there’s even medium-length lag, you can buy a lot of moderation in a ~year.

  2. The leftists and liberals who march with Trump. It’s no great secret of history that extremist movements feed on each other. Nationalists vs communists in China, Germany, and Spain in the 20th Century; Zionists vs Hamas; Bush-era hawks vs Al-Qaeda; probably more ethnic conflicts than I can count. The excesses of one side always justify the excesses of the other. If one side suddenly disappeared, the other would lose all its rhetorical force and a lot of its support. Obviously sides to polarized conflicts like these can be more or less defensible or grounded in reality. The left is much more reasonable than the right in practice, which is one reason I would like to appeal to them to rein in their excesses if possible. On the margin, that’s doing a lot more to help Trump than it is to help them. In addition to creating easy targets for the right (and not repudiating most of the easy targets), there is also purity-policing your own side: kicking out natural allies for not being closely aligned enough to your substantive vision. I’m glad to see some of this latter dynamic on the right lately, but we can always do better ourselves.

  3. Why decent people don’t see that Trump is evil. This will be a list post that reflects the reality that there’s no single explanation. People have a bunch of beliefs and judgements and information gaps that combine and net out to broad support for Trump. These include: simple “team R” tribal dynamics; assuming there are two sides to every story; specific confusions about trade and labor economics; Trump’s relatability; not knowing what due process is; assuming judges are political actors like anyone else, and more…

  4. Freedom bots. If you know Twitter (currently X) — and I know Twitter — you know that it’s overrun with right wing bots. Basically every comment section on every post about US politics is 40% vile and/or conspiratorial comments from KYDogMom449, TampaTurf, or BigVets4Trump. All AI generated profile pictures, most accounts opened in 2022 or more recently and have 10,000+ posts (i.e. 10+ posts every, single day for years). Always negative/antagonistic, always extreme. I assume these are run by some combination of Russia, China, and private MAGA groups in America. Comments saying simple, true, relevant things like “I think Biden won the 2020 election,” or “I don’t think the country is about to collapse,” are vanishingly rare by comparison, despite reflecting what most people think. I suspect this is downstream of fair-minded people being unwilling to spin up their own bot farms. Someone should be willing to sully themselves in this way to keep the public’s perception of the public’s perception from being further distorted.

  5. Political credibility scores. Wherein I make a quiz filled with politically relevant facts, figures, and concepts. How well you do on this tells you something about how qualified you are to opine on politics. I have no clever mechanism to enforce honest reporting of scores, but perhaps some people would take some pause if they got an exceptionally low score. I jotted down the first few things that came to mind here.

  6. The Trump administration wants ICE officers to be attacked. I could use a stronger word than attacked. The administration is spending tens of billions to send new, untrained, masked men onto American streets where they are told to employ extremely aggressive and indiscriminate tactics all to achieve a very average deportation rate compared to past administrations. It’s possible they believe this will successfully directly intimidate both immigrants and their political opponents into backing off of criticism, but I think it is more likely they are trying to instigate violence against their own officers. We saw how eagerly and opportunistically the Trump administration leapt at the chance to use Charlie Kirk’s murder to villainize their enemies. Attacks on ICE officers could be used just the same way. I think it is good to disseminate this hypothesis because it both discourages violence and thereby makes the whole scheme less likely to work. Perhaps I can say more about how the Trump administration has narratively positioned itself to benefit from chaos and decline.

  7. Why there’s no centrist Rogan. A big part of Joe Rogan’s (and many others’) charisma comes from their willingness to speculate wildly about all manner of things they don’t know and to do so with great confidence. They trust their own intuitions. They think they’re onto something. It’s exciting. It’s also how most people relate to the world. When a big issue surfaces to their attention, the thing they want is something interesting or controversial to say. It will win them some attention. It might even subconsciously serve to let them know who likes them for them (i.e. is willing to entertain nonsense just because it’s coming from their mouth). The problem with moderates is that they insist on staying in their lane, expressing uncertainty, and deferring to experts. That’s no fun! I want to come up with a bunch of (directionally) true takes that are interesting and can be spouted off with bravado. This is to say nothing of the perhaps bigger need to disagree with particular beliefs while validating the people who hold them (as opposed to labeling them dangerous spreaders of disinformation).

  8. Trumpism might be immune to ideological Turing tests. I’m overstating it with the title, but I have a Gettier-type problem with steelmanning Trumpism. I can say the words that will convince a Trumpist that I understand where they’re coming from with maximal detail (I will do that as part of the post and you can judge), but I will not in fact be moved even a little bit towards sympathy with the policy program, nor will I even understand the appeal, with the possible exception of satisfying some “burn it all down” rage. Otherwise, the policy program concretely benefits no one. Maybe seeing whether I fail the test itself will soften this view.

  9. Why were there so many asylum seekers during the Biden Administration? It looks like internal DHS policies and some executive orders encouraging more and faster humanitarian paroling policies. I want to dig in deeper and see if I can figure out how naïve this was.

  10. Watch the god-damned Super Bowl. Probably listen to Taylor Swift. More importantly, spend 2-3x more energy discussing these in public. I think spending 15 hours per year trying to indulge the most broadly shared parts of the culture is important for being a good liberal. You will mellow out and perhaps others will too.

  11. Wokism as an autoimmune disease. It’s not exactly an original take that many on the social justice left regarded themselves as the inheritors of the civil rights movement and that this led to some excessive self-righteousness about e.g. pronouns and microaggressions. I personally think that most social justice folks would in fact be productive members of the civil rights movement if they lived in the 60s and that their main problem was simply being politically active in the 2010s — an admittedly quite rare period where there was no legitimate oppression to fight. Some people just have a revolutionary, fight-the-power aesthetic. Given that we as a species are prone to repressive authoritarianism, I’m glad this disposition is around. If it’s a constant force in the world, though, it will sometimes misfire, sending out a wave of rage and hostility that engenders backlash from regular people.

  12. The lie at the heart of liberal politics. Liberals often insist on deep natural equality between all individuals such that, in a fair environment, anyone can do anything. The unequal outcomes we observe are all the result of unjust historical contingencies. What people hear liberals saying here is: “when we’re in charge, group x and group y will thrive because fairness and equality will reign.” Against a backdrop that contains some immutable-by-policy differences in both individual and group outcomes, this has a couple of effects. First, if you’re not a part of group x or y, that’s an instant trigger — you don’t think you’re thriving and now the liberals are going to make things harder for you to help somebody else. Second, many members of groups x and y won’t make it, and they’ll perceive a broken promise. Compare this to the right wing vibe of “we’re gonna be big strong and kick ass and let the chips fall where they may.” Chips falling where they may is what people observe under almost any circumstance, so, while people aren’t happy, at least you weren’t robbing or bullshitting them. Of course this makes voters sound very zero sum and sensitive to loss aversion (“have I been explicitly taxed?”), but we go to politics with the minds we have.

You can see that I have decided to win. I hope you will too.

1

Though, to be clear, the takes are not particularly good either.

item.title: Friendship is Optimal for Growing EA
item.description: Affinity is all you need
item.content:encoded:
The dominant memes in Effective Altruism community building are “get people to consider an impactful career,” “get people to take jobs at high impact orgs,” and “get people to donate to high impact orgs.” Those seem great, but I think the most immediate, proximate focus of community builders should be “make sure my members have 3-6 mutually close EA friends.”

Why social circles matter

The problem with directly asking people to work at or donate to some set of places — even if accompanied by a great argument — is that no one cares what you think. People care what their friends think. The number one way people hear about EA is through personal [friends], with local groups providing a strong showing as well:

Moreover, I suspect that everything else on the chart is mediated by people’s social circles. For example, I would answer Astral Codex Ten on this survey, but I never would have taken the survey (or done anything with the nice ideas I found on SSC) if I didn’t run into my law school EA group over a year after I started reading SSC.

Despite really liking Scott’s ideas and arguments about EA, it just didn’t make sense for me to start writing checks or pursuing jobs when there was no one in my life who would care that I did those things beyond a “that’s neat” or “good for you, Matt.” And this is to speak only of initial activation energy. I haven’t even touched on sustaining these habits over years. Find a non-impactful job you’re comfortable with? What are the odds you’ll start a new search on your own initiative? Get nervous about money at some point and don’t donate? Don’t worry, we’ll… send you a reminder email? Having someone who cares about these things to actually talk with sounds vastly more effective.

I don’t doubt that there are saints in the world who respond to moral arguments by effectively binding themselves to do what’s right from now until forever — indeed, I’ve had the privilege of meeting some of them — but relying on these types is not going to scale.

Beyond the straightforward offer of social rewards, focusing on forming small groups around EA ideas also preserves fidelity in the ideas themselves. If you’re just passively consuming intellectual content, you can interpret it however you want. It’s not until you have another smart person whose opinion matters to you that you’ll take disagreement seriously or be willing to genuinely ask a [dumb] question and make the effort to learn the answer. Chances are only 1 in 5 people who like EA ideas is going to have the time to go deep on them anyway.

Being less monolithic about career choice can be good for career changes

These two rationales are part of why I don’t like the implicit “jobs first” framing of EA. That framing ties belonging in EA to hirability by top orgs. If people have accurate views about how hirable they are (which we should all want), they’re only going to provide EA-centric social support to hirable people if they, the support-givers, are also hirable. Assuming these social motivations are decisive, that means you only ever get to hire the best-possible people when they all conveniently arrange themselves into groups of five. That is… unrealistic.

Now maybe this is confusing because it has been true that people hired so far have had friend groups like these. But this is survivorship bias. Even those hires themselves will admit (and not even out of modesty) that they are not the single best candidate on earth for their job. That person didn’t apply. And per my story above, one reason they didn’t apply is because their friends — the people whose opinions they care about — wouldn’t consider such a job. Those hypothetical friends might consider donating though, if that were raised in status. Being an enthusiastic subscriber to Asterisk Magazine or the like might even be enough (again, assuming that’s the kind of thing for which we drummed up enthusiasm).

A world awash in impressive, high-context EAs is a world with many more solid, medium-context EAs egging them on. For that, you need to offer attractive alternatives to roles at orgs.

How to do this

I think current practices are somewhat close to what you’d want to do. It’s sometimes said that “the output of a group is its organizers,” meaning that assembling volunteer groups whose nominal focus is pitching their fellow students or city-dwellers on impactful jobs is actually about getting the volunteer group to pitch themselves in the process. Having a shared project of pitching third parties gives the group something to bond over and an excuse to focus on the ideas and learn about the ecosystem.

All you need to do is be a bit more explicit with organizers that their mission is to spend time playing with the ideas in whatever way best causes people to invest social time and energy into them. This broader framing gives more people more permission to spend that time than the jobs framing. Talk about donation opportunities, debate philosophical edge cases, write meta-level think pieces, follow the news, run a pledge drive. People who take these things seriously in a social setting for a couple years will notice when relevant jobs come up and feel motivated to jump at them when it’s a good fit. Having lower stakes activities like these will cause many more people to keep their heads up in this way.

This is fine

Asking people to leverage their personal relationships for “institutional” goals feels like crossing a line for some, but I think this is how everyone does everything. Corporate recruiters throw parties for ivy leaguers and give the interns mentors who take them out for lunch and shoot the breeze. People end up spending much of their time in an office where their adult social life is shaped around the latest gossip or industry news. Plenty of other people meet their closest friends in church groups or sports bars. We don’t bat an eye at these practices because they’ve been so thoroughly normalized in their respective contexts, but niche new ideas are held to a higher standard because any attempt to emulate these looks “too contrived.”

One way to mitigate the appearance of contrivance and the (potential) reality of manipulation is to be very transparent about this. Everyone can be a part-time recruiter of workers or donors or readers and be celebrated for that. We want people to have fun with these ideas because we know some portion of them will pay it all forward. It doesn’t have to be everyone and no one needs to feel an obligation to do more than is enjoyable for them and their friends. The rewards for stepping up and dedicating your career to this stuff will be modest rather than a steep cliff where people feel chewed up and spit out. Churchgoers and line workers don’t particularly envy priests and middle-managers.

item.title: Why I'm Writing an EA Holy Book
item.description: To get so much into one place
item.content:encoded:
One undercurrent of my 12 theses on EA is that popular EA messages focus too much on effectiveness and not enough on altruism. To rectify this, I’m writing an EA holy book. The book will partly be a compendium of other people’s writings that I have found most compelling on the altruism front, edited for brevity and consistency with each other, and then some things I write up to frame and tie things together.

By “too much on effectiveness and not enough on altruism,” I mean that popular texts like Doing Good Better, The Precipice, or even What We Owe the Future are too focused on facts, figures, and analysis. They’re artifacts of pop intellectualism rather than serious treatises on how we ought to live.

The rationale for these popular books makes sense to me. If you want to reach a wide audience, you should offer them something concrete, like teaching them a bunch of interesting things about the world and some crisp ways of thinking about those facts. It’s also probably important not to be too overtly earnest or absorbed in your own righteousness the way a self-styled holy book might. These texts also make a very friendly-to-the-reader assumption that everyone wants to do good and help others. They’re merely providing new facts and strategies to improve those efforts, rather than calling on readers to make serious change in their lives.

My holy book (sorry I don’t even know what I want to call it yet), by contrast, isn’t aimed at instant appeal or any best seller lists. Like most holy books, it’s there as a resource for the people already committed to its core message. It can remind them of what matters to them, why they make the sacrifices and do the work that they do, and help them stay in touch with the version of themselves they most want to be.

More ambitiously, it might create common knowledge of concepts, principles, and ways of acting that are mutually reinforcing in the community. Again I think the Rationalists have done well here in no small part because they have taken themselves (too?) seriously with things like the twelve virtues of rationality, FDT, reference class tennis, the litany of Gendlin, etc. I have at times been taken aback to learn, for example, that some quite-involved Effective Altruist was not familiar with On Sincerity or the stories in Strangers Drowning.

I even notice in writing this (and asking ChatGPT) that almost all the EA jargon and ~unique concepts are grounded in philosophy and cause prioritization: moral weights/uncertainty, counterfactuals, replaceability, value drift, etc. It’s all very cold and strategic. Cold and strategic have their place of course, and indeed the project of Effective Altruism has largely been about elevating the unduly maligned cold and strategic perspectives that matter to whether people live or die, but I fear this is a symptom of EA doing what all groups do: leaning into what makes it distinctive rather than leaning into an accurate representation of what it actually, most earnestly cares about. There is a lot of overlooked warmth and humanity in that latter category that I hope the holy book will bring out.

With that, here’s my outline (again). I may try to get cracking on it this month as I continue posting, but these will be forced, low quality versions of chapters likely to be re-written wholesale. Still, it’s a start.

item.title: On Being Primates
item.description: Feeling out an early chapter of the new EA canon
item.content:encoded:
I haven’t been emailing posts lately because I haven’t been able to put enough effort into them. All the same, I wanted to start my EA Holy Book project by diving into what I expect to be an early chapter reflecting on what we are, namely, primates.

I feel modestly confident that the five subjects I want to cover are as follows:

  1. Our evolutionary origins

  2. The brutality and cruelty of nature and our history

  3. Epistemic biases

  4. Moral biases

  5. The tiny glimmer of something else

The first four are all factual and build up towards something more normative in the fifth. The hope is to convey the daunting challenge of overcoming our biology to achieve something I think the reader endorses on the deepest level. All the way along I want to convey a lot of sympathy for the reader and for myself. The things that pull on us, attract us, and otherwise make us fall short of perfection are often rooted deep in our biology. That’s both hard to change and something we often — at least on many levels — don’t even want to change.

The bleg portion of this post is mostly looking for good source materials to adapt on each point.

On evolution, I want to be concise. I don’t need this book to be teaching people evolution from first principles. But rather to gesture broadly at some of its basic mechanisms as a way to set up parts three through four. The tone will convey the basics of inclusive genetic fitness while making a nod to the fact that our genes have both made us who we are while at the same time enslaving (parts of) us to serve the end of their proliferation. It seems foolish to swim directly against the evolutionary tide, but at the same time we should be ambitious about our enlightened ability to overcome the worst things it’s done to us, first as individuals making choices about our lives and maybe later as a community and society becoming its best self.

On the brutality and cruelty of history, I imagine some good passages from Joseph Henrich in The Secret of Our Success and possibly WEIRDest People in the World would be helpful. I’d focus on describing the facts about human tribes, conflict, and the basic inhumanity and immorality we demonstrated for long periods of evolutionary history. This could also go as far as speaking to the origins of wars and how those were conducted from a psychological perspective too. How and why did humans do these things given their evolutionary history? I hope this can be done without getting so conceptual as to cannibalize the points I want to make under the moral and epistemic bias headings.

Epistemic biases will maybe be the easiest section to find options for source material, but the hardest to make concise. Here, I’d just be looking for general materials explaining all the various epistemic biases we have, and why we have them, why they persist, and why they’re hard to overcome. I suspect it’ll also be hard to match the more reverent tone of the rest of the book in this section where most popular discussions skew much more technical and educational. Maybe the way to go about this is to emphasize how these biases make us somewhat helpless at recognizing what we most want and soberly connecting our intentions to our actions when doing so comes at a selfish cost.

Moral biases will build on this by calling back to the brutality and cruelty section, but it will be clearer about the ways in which things that were horrifying in the past are still with us in more mundane ways today. The hope is that drawing that connection will help motivate people to counteract them more earnestly.

The tiny glimmer of something else reflects a hope for overcoming these challenges, daunting as they might be, and is what I wrote about in my Tiny Flicker of Altruism post. Somehow we’re able to see past these constraints and imagine a world where they don’t bind. Perhaps we’ve even made real progress in overcoming them in some domains. How did that happen? And how can you, the reader, summon in yourself what you need to continue what progress we’ve already seen, and reach the world that the best version of yourself actually wants?

item.title: A Spectrum of Reasons for Being EA
item.description: Good, Bad, and Neutral
item.content:encoded:
I’m an Effective Altruist, but I say so predominantly because that’s the way most people use those words, not because giving people labels or putting them in buckets is especially important to me. That said, these words are useful to me in the sense that I want to be able to say there are a lot more Effective Altruists in the world. Having met some, I have some thoughts about the most primal things that might be motivating them.

As with all my non-emailed posts in November, I turned this one out really fast and I don’t endorse you reading it. Perhaps I’ll feel differently when I have time to write a remastered version of this post next year. With that out of the way:

The Flattering

Reflective empathy

You watch factory farm footage. You see a family member suffer intensely from disease. You ask why things have to be this way. You ask what you can do to make things different. You take the responses you get from yourself and from others seriously. You understand that what’s wrong here is not the particular circumstances you witnessed, but the suffering itself is what mattered. You think about how broadly it sweeps. You feel the cost of your limited capacity to help. You get serious about tradeoffs.

Sense of duty/obligation to help others

This might be the most commonly talked-about reason for becoming an EA. These are the people who studied from some philosophy, decided that utilitarianism was right, and that it was their affirmative moral obligation to maximize welfare in the world. For them, the weight of this obligation carries them to extreme frugality and extreme hard-workingness. This has produced some of the best EAs but also some of the worst, with most of the variation being a product of how much realizing the truth of utilitarianism dovetailed with reflective empathy vs pure argumentative elegance.

The Neutral

Desire to solve coordination problems

You’re a bit of a fixer. You like to solve problems and maybe you think too much about politics and policy. You probably study economics or have a long-running libertarian streak that made the efficient market hypothesis intuitive for you. Since risk-adjusted billion-dollar bills aren’t lying on the sidewalk for you, you realize that market failures are the place to go to achieve something great and find no shortage of big opportunities when EA comes along and lists some of them out. Wait, what do you mean this isn’t flattering?

Enjoyment in cognitively challenging community

This is the STEMmy version of the coordination problem solvers. I think EA community builders imagine this category to be potentially a lot bigger than it is. The idea is that the technical features of AI alignment work or vaccine/synthesis screening/diagnostic countermeasures in biosecurity are so appealing to the right kind of nerd that they jump at them or get “nerdsniped” because no one has ever presented a socially useful unsolved technical problem before (I’m not being facetious, that might actually be true). I think this might be a partial draw for some EAs or maybe it was very early on for those who were especially STEMmy, but as time goes on, my sense is that these people filter themselves much more strongly into one of the other categories.

The Unflattering

Happenstance & laziness

Back in EA’s heyday of rapid growth in 2021 and 2022, there was a lot of surface area for young people to look around and see this big, fast-growing movement that had a good story for itself and some enthusiastic advocates. They thought that this was just the natural thing for them to do and the most easy thing to learn about quickly since those community builders were making it so easy for them.

As time went on, they didn’t learn as much about anything else and they sort of just drifted into hoping to get one of these EA jobs. Some of them were naturally gifted and smart enough to land jobs and things worked out fine (but probably not great). For others, I fear they were met with the harsh reality that the bar for hiring at EA orgs — which was the main thing that EA messaging was pushing at that time and still is — was higher than they were led to believe. This latter group either became disaffected or showed great maturity into settling into a non-EA job and continuing to follow EA from perhaps a slightly greater distance.

Social pressure

Social pressure is a closely related phenomenon that also cropped up in the heyday of rapid EA growth. If you ran into one of those enthusiastic community builders or had a few too many discussions about what your obligations actually were or should be, you felt guilty about ignoring all this effort your friends and advisors put into supporting you and you increasingly framed your goals in an EA light. If you don’t end up working at an EA org, there’s a good chance you’ll drift away from EA and earning to give, but maybe I’m too cynical here.

Recognizing this as a game you could win

Sorry I’m going to end on an even more cynical note. One personal theory of mine is that some of the best and most talented EAs subconsciously looked around and realized that they were not going to be at the absolute top of their class. President, Congressman, chairman of the firm were not on the cards for them. But they recognized that they were still quite impressive and — rather than always being runner-up in society’s primary competition for wealth and power — they chose a smaller, but still reasonably interesting and impressive pond in which to be a bigger fish. EA, with its well educated fan base, neat ideas, and reasonably large amount of money, fit the bill.

Those are the motives/typologies I came up with in thinking about this for 15 minutes. Mine is mostly a coordination problems and social pressure story, though I’m working on my reflective empathy. Do let me know what categories I missed completely though.

item.title: 14 Components of my World Model
item.description: Bosses, taxes, and Big History futurism
item.content:encoded:
Your world model is the set of beliefs you have about how the world works at a basic level. The contents of people’s world models are the largest determinant of why they disagree about what’s important and what people ought to be doing.

Typically, the beliefs discussed under the heading “world model” are more specific than the laws of physics and more general than claims like “we should break up Amazon.” They’re the often-unstated premises of the arguments you make. When you notice these premises, state them, and see the work they’re doing in forming object-level beliefs, your thinking improves and the quality of your arguments goes way up. When you think carefully about what the components of a world model ought to be and choose wisely, things get better still.

Sadly what follows are not my most fundamental, load-bearing world model components, but the ones I thought were niche and under-discussed enough to make for novel blogposts:

  1. The future is a loaded gun. People in my circles have already written ad nauseam about how we’re at a very unusual point in history. We’re on the end of two centuries of explosive growth by the standards of human history and still exploding. Slightly less demonstrable is the specific dry powder we’ve been accumulating in the last two decades. Obviously AI could set off an intelligence explosion, but even failing that, we would have a massive compute overhang from today’s AI buildup and the continually more-sophisticated chips. Someone will figure something out. Backstopping even that is biology. The wild cheapness of DNA sequencing; our rapidly expanding knowledge of polygenetic traits; CRISPR; protein folding… It’s not exactly rubbing two sticks together, but all the tools for a biological intelligence explosion are already here and I don’t think today’s squeamishness persists forever.

  2. People will give up their traditions when something better comes along. People are often pessimistic about meat alternatives because eating flesh is so deeply ingrained in our history and culture. Putting aside the fact that eating it at the scale we do now is an extremely recent phenomenon, I think we’ve seen plenty of customs fall away in the wake of only modestly better alternatives. Church attendance, newspaper reading, even TV watching fell away precipitously in single generations. People would rather use social media. You can argue whether phones and social media retain too many of the essential features of the things they replaced, but that’s kind of the whole idea of meat alternatives. Perhaps newspapers, TV, and church are all too recent in evolutionary history to have really stuck in. If so, I might need to look into the extent that men have given up sex for porn. I’m confident that pre-dates meat consumption.

  3. The moral imperative of being a chill dude. It seems like we’re surrounded by emotional purity death spirals right, left, and other. Trump sues the owner of Fox News for not glazing him hard enough; 100% vegans think 99% vegans are serial killers; every conceivable offense against wokism is cause to ruin your life. These heated purity fights clearly dominate the attention market, but what they do collectively does not reflect strength on the margin. They are all preaching to the converted, or trying to get out the (very close) vote. Actual, robust change comes from people changing their minds, which, when it happens, happens only incrementally and in response to new information, usefully presented. Your typical deconverted rightwing extremist is going to look a lot more like Richard Hanania than Robin DiAngelo. Moralizing and browbeating doesn’t work. Being patient, positive, helpful and non-judgmental — but still firm in your convictions — does. See also Guided by the Beauty of Our Weapons.

  4. The 80th percentile academic is just a teacher. People vastly overrate professors. It is true that once you have tenure, you can in theory use the job as a platform for independent writing and impact, but hardly anyone even tries that. These are mostly just people who went to grad school and kept writing papers. They got a job a lot of people wanted through some combination of luck and being relatively good. Fundamentally, they’re just writing grad student papers on their own initiative, which isn’t nothing — people are very lazy — but it isn’t much either. The evidence is in the download counts. Even other academics would much rather read a blog.

  5. Don’t try to be all things to all people with advice. A lot of impressive, experienced people have hot takes and gut level reactions to mistakes people are making in their field or in choosing/developing careers (and lives) generally. Whenever I hear impressive people give advice though, it’s incredibly generic and clichéd. Then, to the extent things get meaningfully opinionated, there’s a ton of hedging about who it might and might not apply to with a bunch of precautionary measures you should take before applying it (“talk to your doctor” etc). People should instead make a best guess about who’s listening to them and then be very direct about what you think is good or bad or overrated or underrated. If people can’t figure out how it applies to their situation, I don’t think there was much hope for them anyway. Stop treating false-negative minimization as your north star!

  6. Selection effects rule everything around you. The people you see in a given context and the things they do there are all determined by the features of that environment that precluded different people or behaviors from being there. It’d be great if the local McDonald’s had a wise, patient, fatherly assistant manager — so much better for the employees and the customers. Unfortunately, there are too many alternative places of employment that offer more pay and more social status to people with those qualities such that none are left to work at McDonald’s. EA orgs have a similar problem where so few people: 1) understand the ideas, 2) are aware of EA opportunities, and 3) can win the trust of funders, that they have very little competitive pressure to crush it on all fronts. Here, I’ll contrast my experience at EA orgs with my experience at my law firm where the latter was a much thicker market and I found it hard to imagine clear areas for improvement.

  7. People work best with autonomy and skin in the game. The whole idea of hiring someone to do something relies on the person you hire knowing things you don’t and being able to do things you can’t. The best bosses get buy-in on a high level vision and let people do their thing. Part of this is accepting deviation from a precise vision — doing otherwise trades off hard against buy-in and, without buy-in, you quickly face specification gaming: what’s the least I need to do to make the boss happy and collect my pay? This is not the attitude that produces great work, but it is the attitude most micromanagers invite. This is also part of what makes slave economies poor economies, though the size of the tax varies based on specific economic circumstances.

  8. Caring is the scarcest resource in the world. Per above, if a boss doesn’t care enough to have a vision or get buy-in, his report won’t care enough to make use of their knowledge and skills, and so on down the line. “We pretend to work and they pretend to pay us.” The thing that breaks this cycle and sets off a positive feedback loop is someone in the chain caring enough about what happens on the ground that they do what’s needed to get others to care too. Since “what can I get away with” is humans’ default attitude to work, this kind of caring is rare.

  9. Greatness exists. This is trivially and obviously true. Read some biographies, watch sports, consider how hard it is to do most complicated, high-stakes things. Despite this, there are people who claim outcomes are driven entirely by good circumstances of birth and plain good luck. No doubt those things matter and help, but none of them push you to put in 80 hour weeks building something incredible for years on end well after you’re a millionaire. Certainly none of them give you the out-of-sample mental agility to come up with whole new paradigms or technology or thinking. The strong cynical take is fundamentally political. It’s there to tell you that you are just as entitled to greatness (and its rewards) as anyone, if only you give a little social power to the cynic. Don’t fall for it.

  10. Greatness happens when people over-do it. We’re generally pretty poorly calibrated on the scale of effort needed to accomplish something in this modern world that we didn’t evolve for. When impressive, new, ground-breaking things happen, it’s usually the product of obsession. Some people get compelled to turn over every stone, answer every question, fight every battle, try every version of an experiment far beyond what we would naïvely predict was sufficient to e.g. make a good product or win an election. And perhaps there are theoretical answers to what is “sufficient,” but I suspect the 80/20 mentality of “just do what’s needed” makes us default to undershooting by a large margin. Much like people are poorly calibrated forecasters who tend to think things are either “near certain” or “unknowable,” we might only have two tracks for effort “just enough (read: lazy)” and “obsessed.”

  11. A fundamental moral question of our age is whether we should fight to preserve the dream time. Most species at most times are in malthusian traps and there’s a clear story about how we fall back into our own malthusian trap. We stumbled into a good situation (the “dream time” where there are far more resources than people to exhaust them) and it’s only by virtue of slowness and other quirks of evolution that our generation experiences the world this way. There are two questions that confront us: 1) whether it’s right to preserve the dream time (i.e. do we reject the repugnant conclusion? Would we violate some important moral side constraint or principle of pluralism by trying to stop people from competing away our bounty?) and 2) whether it’s possible to preserve the dream time (are attempts to push back against evolutionary and competitive pressures doomed to failure in practice?).

  12. Benevolently allocating money means taking views on consumption vs investment tradeoffs. If utility is what you care about and you have zero moral discount rate, should all dollars above subsistence be going into R&D until we reach technological maturity? There’s an interesting question about whether R&D requires robust consumption for feedback on what inventions are useful/most likely to be efficiently climbing the tech tree, but this probably doesn’t concern the very-marginal benevolent investor — there are plenty enough selfish consumers in the world to cover that. It seems like populations at technological maturity are large enough to offset any hedging you want to do by picking up even very low-hanging consumption fruit today (e.g. saving lives from malaria or factory farms), but perhaps your view of future history and the feedback mechanisms involved is not confident enough to justify going all in, especially if it’s unclear where specifically to invest to best contribute to technological feedback loops. This will also be a redux of “is Instacart better than GiveWell?”

  13. Absurdity taxes are real. At least some true things are so insane that ordinary discourse treats them as fiction. Vegan activists often get similar social treatment to conspiracy theorists even though virtually no one denies what they say. The idea that we’re systematically torturing billions of animals who we would never treat badly in person and doing it in a style reminiscent of the holocaust is just a little too out there. It’s probably not as bad as they say, but let’s not look just in case this $5 chicken actually is too good to be true. One could say the same of child mortality in Africa — surely there’s nothing we could do. Their conditions are just too distant and impenetrable, their regimes too corrupt, etc. Similarly with AI in regard to whether we’re living in a normal period or a sci-fi one relative to human history. Educated people who are experts in neither computer science nor economics seem confident the technology is nothing to fret over.

  14. Money, comfort, ideology. Mark Andreessen had a fun taxonomy of things that motivate people: money, love, and force. “Money, comfort, ideology” is the gloss I put on this in an EA context. The kind of “love” at stake in EA is sufficiently specific and filtered through reflection that I feel more comfortable calling it ideology. At some level, love is a story we tell ourselves about how we relate to specific others that taps a powerful emotion. At some point, we filter the emotion (what we fundamentally care about) through enough storytelling that ideology becomes a better word. EA orgs also have some amount of money to offer people, but considerably more flexibility on how attractive the working environment is, i.e “comfort.” On Mark’s story, comfort and money trade off on a 1-1 basis such that you don’t need to decompose them. That might be less true for us. I wonder whether we’re optimizing these motivational tools. I think we’ve neglected ideology of late, in part because we’ve bullied ourselves into treating it like a dirty word.

item.title: We Are Always Talent/Idea Constrained
item.description: Trillions have been earned; it's you job to give them something worth giving to
item.content:encoded:
I recently had a chat with some of the friendly folks at Open Philanthropy about their perpetual conundrum: how to turn money into value. Now you might respond to this by saying, “Oh, it must be easy! Just give all the money to <insert idea the speaker likes>.” To this I’d respond, “Well, have you considered that your idea, like almost all ideas, is bad? And that you don’t have amazing people to execute on it?”1

This is Frontier Analysis. Most things don’t work. Even most things people try don’t work. Even most things that do work don’t work that well. Open Phil and others, I speculate, are keeping some of their powder dry in hopes they come across things that work really well to make the world a better place.

Just look at the AI safety landscape. Open Phil funds a bunch of prosaic technical safety and alignment research or wonkish palatable-to-industry policy ideas, both grounded in today’s models, which might not even be very good model organisms for the future models we’re actually worried about. The rationalists point out that this seems like incredibly weak medicine to avoid human extinction at the hands of superintelligence, and that Open Phil is wasting its money.

For themselves, the rationalists think it’s wiser to try to wake up broad swathes of the public to the fact that AI is going to kill us all soon and that we ought to simply coordinate and shut down frontier development — an admitted long shot of a proposition whose only virtue is that it at least works conditional on getting the coordination in the first place.

The only reason either of these strategies makes any sense to anyone is because the prize at the end — avoiding human extinction and/or securing a vast, flourishing, long-term future — is big enough. The bar for the promisingness of interventions with smaller prizes like improving air quality or advancing meat alternatives is even higher. And perhaps it should be, given the relatively straightforward nature of those problems. Things like air quality and meat alternative speak especially strongly to the overall issue though, because it’s exactly in these comprehensible, low stakes places that we’ve seen so many things not work at all.

Against this backdrop, I see EAs getting excited about the prospect of securing new billionaire funders for the causes we care about. But the point above is that money doesn’t really do causes any good. Money does interventions good, by scaling them up, assuming the interventions help (a lot) in the first place. If you don’t have those, you shouldn’t be so concerned about how much money is ready to be deployed in theory.

We’ve even lived through this at least once before. In the FTX era, money was deployed profligately in hopes of leading to good projects and good ideas, which relatively rarely materialized in the wake of that money.

It’s an “if they come, we will build it” mentality, and it runs counter to my basic story of EA’s most compounding and foundational success.

GiveWell started on a comparative shoestring. Just two guys trying to do the rough and ready research to get the best answer they could generate to a question they thought was important: how do we scalably save the most lives for the fewest dollars? Their rough-and-ready answers and the packaging they put around them were good enough that a billionaire couple decided this was the kind of insight they wanted to guide their giving.

Fast forward a little over a decade, and most people in EA’s orbit want assurances that they’ll have high levels of long-term funding before they do their rough and ready MVP or even prioritize building pitches for MVPs.

And look, I know it’s hard to come up with good ideas and even harder to make them concrete enough to be something you could make into a compelling pitch. And it’s harder still to line up the right people with the right backgrounds, raw talent, chemistry, and trustworthiness to turn early funding into scale. I just don’t see having the funding (implicitly) promised up front as making any of that much easier. It probably makes the later stages of this even harder because you get adverse selection for people who see dollar signs.

So I expect most people who try to do this to fail. The low hanging fruit in social good is less picked-over than that in areas where you can generate big profits, but it’s still very hard to find and effort alone is no guarantee. Still, I don’t want people to give up on doing or supporting good things — or being a part of a community that does — just because they haven’t succeeded in what I’ve defined as “the thing” here (seeding new impactful projects through direct work). More successes means more trials and failures too.

My point is that the risk of failure high because for reasons other than funding. There’s $5.2 trillion in savings in the US. All of it is looking for the right consumption or investment opportunity.2 $600 billion of that goes to charity every year and yes, I know, religion and universities etc etc, but you’re telling me you can’t pitch a plan and a team well enough to get a hearing from even 1% of that (in hopes of landing 0.001% of that)? That you’re waiting for some (additional!) billionaire to spontaneously declare sympathy with your perspective first? Or for one of your friends to win the lottery (read: cash in their AI equity)?

The lesson of GiveWell is that great direct work doesn’t draw down some fixed pot of EA money or tradeoff with earning to give; it provides the proof of concept that makes new funders excited to take more risk with EA projects and incubate them for longer. Accordingly, I see the driver of really great projects as having courage in your convictions despite the absence of pre-committed funding.

So in an appalling display of laziness and mild hypocrisy, I’m getting to work on my project of helping people find the courage of those convictions. More to come.

1

Disclosure: my own idea is mid, but I might have an amazing person to execute on it.

2

Yes you heard me right, your impactful org doesn’t even have to be a nonprofit

item.title: Saying The Simpler, Truer Thing
item.description: On Pedantry
item.content:encoded:
This is another bleg for my EA holy book wherein I want to have a chapter on pedantry. I couldn’t find a good source for this on LessWrong, so I’m very interested to know if readers have recommendations that make the case I try to make here, but better. Even just examples of people practicing the craft I describe here would be very helpful.

It is good to be precise; it is good to be correct. Rather than these, people are too often interested in feeling righteous or asserting social dominance. I’ve noticed some rationalists have cured this in themselves and I want to describe the particular practice of pedantry that I think helps them find truth and improve discourse in more detail.

The good practice of pedantry embraces plain, precise speech and suppression of normative attitudes. Mr. Spock, the oft-objectified alien from a cold, strictly logical world, embodies two qualities as he acts to temper the hot-blooded emotionality of his ship’s predominantly human crew. Spock doesn’t leap to conclusions or rely on heuristics like deference to his political allies. He slows down and calculates. It’s rare that he asserts an all-things-considered judgement about what to do even after he’s thought about a problem. Instead, he just states the connection between proposed actions and their likely outcomes, and makes the more decisive crew members grapple with the implications of their more moralized stances.

These practices of plain speech and holding back emotionality will cause you to do a lot less explicit side-taking and conclusion-stating. The “explicit” is important here, because plainly stated, uncolored facts often speak for themselves. It’s obvious what conclusion to draw from a statement like “This data center uses 4000x less water than you claimed it did,” namely, that claims about AI and water use are sometimes poorly evidenced. That general point is often more persuasive when left unsaid. For better or worse, people are quite attached to their beliefs, especially their more general beliefs. When you come right out and say “AI’s water use isn’t important,” or worse “AI isn’t bad for the environment,” people’s defenses rise because an important view of theirs is directly under attack. The narrower, harder-to-deny claim by itself does this much less and takes people out of fight-or-flight mode with regard to their important, high-level belief and lets them slowly, comfortably ratchet their credence in that belief up or down as they see more pieces of evidence.

Cherishing this virtue of pedantry is probably even better for the speaker. Knowing that you’ve bound yourself to speak pedantically takes you further away from high-level, identity-bearing beliefs even faster. You are what you do. If you operate in specific, narrow claims about specific, narrow topics, the grip of overarching narratives and identities will hold you less tightly.

Similarly, emphasizing precise narrow claims more often invites your five senses to falsify them in a way that is much more challenging with grand abstractions. Knowing this, you’re less inclined to make things up. The potential for highly-legible embarrassment afterwards is too high. This means you’ll more often say you don’t know things, at least when you first consider them. This is first a cue for you to actually learn the thing you don’t know. Second, it is a helpful reminder of how vast the space of things you and, by extension, others don’t know. Given that reality needs to collapse into some coherent web of facts, the fact that there is so much we don’t know is humbling. It can drive us to be better, more open, less hostile listeners for what is true.

If that virtue is contagious, a great fog that hangs over all of us begins to lift. We can start working together to understand things as they are instead of what they say about us.

item.title: The Will to Obsolescence
item.description: We should all long to earn to give
item.content:encoded:
It should be a sad thing to realize that you, through your direct work, are in a uniquely strong position to make a better world. For one thing, it is a grave responsibility. For another, it means that the systems that exist for finding and securing people to do such work were unable to find anyone better than you.

For any such role, it is very likely that there is such a person. The field of high leverage do-gooding is small, and lacks the reach to find the literal strongest candidates on Earth. And even if there is no one better than you, you should still feel a residual sadness that no one better for this role exists. The world’s problems persist because we lack some combination of sufficiently powerful angels and geniuses. Given that we’re all (hopefully) intimately familiar with our personal limitations, it becomes easy for someone at the frontier of work in bettering the world to imagine someone better equipped to handle their task, if only in small ways.

At the same time, given the responsibility at stake, it’s important not to let this sadness pervade your thoughts. You’ll need energy and enthusiasm to meet the challenge of doing the best you can in this project. The premise was always that the world was broken in some important ways, and if you weren’t going to let that get you down, you shouldn’t let this particular facet of the world’s brokenness get you down either. We all know the pragmatic thing to do is to turn to the day-to-day, get things done, and not dwell on our cosmic position.

Therein lies the challenge, though. Organizations run on people and relationships, including relationships that cut across organizations and reach out into the world. Organizations need proud and confident representatives. They need those to grow, build partnerships, and influence the course of events. It is efficient and even desirable that you immerse yourself in your role — especially when your role is an important one — and embrace these aspects of personality that are relevant to it.

In doing this, you run a serious risk of fully forgetting that you aren’t the best person in the world to be doing what you’re doing. And if you do that — however unconsciously — you’ll start to build walls up around your role and around your organization that deter the best person from coming forward. It appears clearer and clearer who the bosses are in this corner of the world and what assumptions they operate on. Part of the reason you’re not the best person for your job is that your assumptions might not be the best ones. Those potentially erroneous assumptions, however, might appear set in stone to a perceptive would-be collaborator. And so those scarce and precious resources devoted to your project get cloistered away, bound to assumptions whose originators can’t see they’ve erred.

So while you shouldn’t dwell on the state of the world all the time, you do need some mechanisms to guard against becoming the mask you put on to serve the world too. Those mechanisms look like dedicating part of your time to revisiting first principles arguments about what’s important. You should go out and make those arguments to people who lack all the specific context and assumptions you’ve accumulated. The arguments should ground all the way out to the exact strategy you’re taking to solve the problem.

You should also have people closer to your project who share your context but who are less attached to it test the core assumptions with others far beyond the walls of your project. If you’re wrong about something important, your replacement might be the one who points it out, or — more likely — they might be drawn to work with you when you’ve course corrected. But they’ll only do so if you create surface area for that.

This is all the more true when your view is a lonely one. People are familiar with animal welfare and global health challenges, for example. They are familiar despite neglecting those problems, so the problems are both more important to work on and less important to be worried about missing something critical. The world has looked at these problems and failed on them only morally. Moral arguments are much harder to make and, in these cases, there seems to be a genuine acceptance that akrasia is the issue.

On an issue like AI risk, where the arguments are complicated and world-model dependent, the situation is importantly different. Its complex nature calls for even more frequent reevaluation of strategy. Its comparative obscurity calls for even more effort to make the simplest case in a clear way before you appoint yourself — as the one who’s thought about it the longest so far — the chief architect of any solution.

I hope both inviting debate and reevaluating project assumptions can be done joyfully, with longing for the day a torch can be passed from the vigilant, concerned early adopters to the truly excellent leaders they found. Vigilance and concern are great qualities to reserve for first principles reasoning and prioritization, so if you were selected for having these in spades, perhaps that’s evidence you should return to and thrive in the arena of uncovering new priorities or supporting the efforts that execute on them, rather than leading and creating those efforts in perpetuity yourself.

item.title: On Being Mortal
item.description: EA Holy Book Series #1
item.content:encoded:
The text below is a draft introduction to the first chapter of my as yet unnamed EA Holy Book project. I planned for the section to predominately be made up of a very lightly edited version of Joe Carlsmith’s Thoughts on Being Mortal,1 but I may borrow more from the primary source material once I read through it.

Death is always with us, whether we dwell on it or not.

As you open this book, reflect on what it will be like to have closed the book of your life. The particular circumstances of that moment—death—will be different for everyone, but there are some universals. You will have done all that you will do in this world. You’ll no longer be able to act or speak or witness the things that matter to you.

No one and no thing will be able to touch you, teach you, or make you feel something. The people you’ve connected with will start thinking of you in more summary, essentialist terms. Then they will think about you less, and then not at all. Wherever your relationships stood when you died will get frozen there. Whatever memories you will have made by then will be all there is. Whatever you spoke last to someone will be, for them, your final goodbye.

Already, some of your past may have a feeling of finality to it: you’ve done what you’ve done and can’t take it back. There is still much you can do about what you’ve done though. You can explain. You can make up for wrongs or call in favors. You can tell your own story from your own mouth and hope to move others. You can take new actions that build on old foundations whose structure and purpose are understood uniquely by you.

Then, at a specific moment in time, all those options permanently disappear. At that instant, the “true” story of your life will have been written. Others may go on to discuss and reinterpret who you were or what you did and they’ll form their own views – they do that now. The difference will be that you will have no power to change what they think. More importantly, you’ll have no power to change what you think about your life. True – you won’t be there to regret anything, or to celebrate anything, but you can imagine your current self observing that future moment. You will have a view. You have a view now, knowing the person you’ve been and the person you are shaping up to be. You can imagine what it will be like to know there’s no more later to do the things that most needed doing.

This book is written to help answer that question: Who do you want to have been? What do you want the character of your scarce waking hours to be? Will today’s hours end up mattering?

You’re forgiven for putting the book down now if you’ve known all along how to make your hours matter and simply needed someone to raise the question again. For most though, the question feels harder than that and worth spending time on. Indeed, the question can sound paralyzing on its face. There are too many perspectives to consider, too many worthy ends and virtues competing for our time to ever know how to adjudicate between them.

And sadly this book and its many authors provide no one, reliable answer. What these passages do is grasp earnestly towards the question. These – effort and earnestness – are at least general features of the things we most want from ourselves. The tentative answers contemplated in these passages center on goodness, helping, and leaving the world something that matters.

That something should reflect a genuine attempt at understanding the world and ourselves. There, the best we can often do is explore what it means to seriously ask the question: Who are we and what is our situation? For one thing, we are primates — physically embodied creatures with a long, long history and all the limitations that come with that. We also live among each other as well as minds quite different than our own. Most importantly, we live in a past whose future will be the product of our actions. Time taken to sit with these questions is usually time we won’t regret, unless we become so preoccupied with the questions themselves that we never experience or affect the world.

So that something we leave the world will also reflect our experience and effect on the world. Because the answers to those earlier questions are never final and always the product of ignorance, we cannot be certain our actions are what we would want if we really understood. Yet we have no choice but to act. The passages that follow will discuss the natural course of things: disease, decay, predation, connection, growth, wisdom. Neglect and omission resign the world to the first three and deny it the last three. Both are choices. To refuse the question is a choice.

The first thing this book seeks to convey is that your life is yours. It is yours and it is finite. It will be what you make of it, or don’t make of it. It will end and that will be that. But what will the ‘what’ and the ‘that’ be?

1

Assuming I got permission

item.title: Memorable Concepts from Replacing Guilt
item.description: Reflecting on the non-self help aspects of a self-help book
item.content:encoded:
Clicking through some of the links involved in writing yesterday’s post led me to some segments of Replacing Guilt/Minding Our Way. Today, I listened through the whole thing in audio form (available on podcast apps) for the first time (I also haven’t read it—yes I know). Just in case you’re in a similar boat of also not having read it, perhaps a couple of these takeaways will motivate you to do so, and I do recommend it.

Specifically, I recommend it in its written form rather than the audio form. I found the audio too easy to tune out from at various points, especially when things seem to be getting repetitive (though the repetition is helpful). The primary thing that makes these essays valuable is your ability to read one paragraph at a time and think of moments where you have fallen prey to one of the various traps that Soares writes about or failed to realize one of the opportunities he points to. The audio form goes by too quickly to really allow for that.

Active choice over apparent defaults

The front matter of the full book—“Half-assing it with everything you’ve got”—discusses the idea of recognizing “preference curves” as the proper object of most of our actions. This stands in contrast to simple defaults of slacking off or going all out towards an arbitrary goal that someone else set for us. An example of an arbitrary goal set by someone else would be getting straight As (with maximum confidence and therefore much wasted effort). An example of slacking off would be simply not doing something, rather than having some specific alternative used for the time and resources that you might have put into the something. Like, for example, getting perfect grades with high confidence.

I’m surprised that the word “default” didn’t appear anywhere in Half-assing It with Everything You’ve Got. This is because I interpret the main thrust of the essay to be about actively choosing the things that matter to you (whatever combination of relaxation and accomplishment those might be), rather than thoughtlessly selecting some action that feels like either the cultural default (slacking) or something specifically laid out by someone else (getting straight As). The vibe of resisting defaults is captured nonetheless, and it sets up much of the rest of the book. For example, the book frequently emphasizes conscious choice, i.e. the “free time” that I’m fighting for needs some specific, concrete object—the thing that I actually want to spend the free time on—as opposed to merely free time, which means freedom from burden (of culturally determined defaults or someone else’s vision for me).

Reality itself

A related theme that Soares hints at early in the book is a deep reverence for reality itself that I think he never makes fully explicit. Rather it comes out in at least three distinct points that Soares harps on.

One is explicitly rejecting nihilism. He does this by disparaging the nihilism of having no specific, concrete goal of your own (as above), rejecting the “nothing really matters” view reflected in tolerizing cynicism (more below), and even quite late in the book, rejecting the notion that there is literally nothing worth going all out for.

Another way Soares manifests his reverence for reality is his preoccupation with rejecting experience machine-type thought experiments. I.e., the section where he talks about whether you would accept the painless death of your pet dog substituted by the illusion of your dog’s continued existence and the erasure of your memory of your actual dog’s painless death.

Third, and more minorly, Soares has some asides where he rejects naïve Cartesianism and its Little Homunculus Man, which seems right. This in turn seems related to his frequent reminders throughout the book that we are our brains, and that our brains are meat computers not designed for the task of either understanding the world or pursuing goals that we would regard as desirable.

Maybe the strongest pronouncement of reverence for reality itself is Soares’s strong suggestion (I won’t say insistence) that the most laudable goals are those that concern the whole future of the multiverse. Elsewhere in the book, Soares makes it reasonably clear that you’re entitled to whatever goals you choose, especially if you reflect well, but I think Soares’s personal conclusion—that the fate of the universe is the important thing—permeates the way of thinking expressed throughout the entire book.

Principles vs felt-experience

Another frequent—and maybe unsurprising—theme was the tension between “rational principles” and our felt experience. This was most explicit when Soares was talking about his care for strangers and everyone who does and will exist. Specifically, Soares points out that our desire for strangers to live happy lives and be respected often sits in tension with how little their existence emotionally resonates with us, let alone their preferences as compared to, say, our close friends and family. Perhaps I missed it, but I don’t think he gives a knock-down argument for minimizing the felt gulf between those two groups. Yes, it’s largely a product of coincidence that we were born into the families we were born into and found the friends we found, so there’s some reason to treat the privilege we naturally give them as arbitrary and worthy of less consideration. But it’s not clear to me why this abstract unattractiveness of arbitrariness gets precedence over what we feel viscerally. To be clear, I give the abstract principles precedence over my gut feelings a lot more than others. I just tend to think that preference is more arbitrary than many who argue it isn’t. I just find the principles beautiful in a narrative sense and I have a vivid imagination.

Still, as a running theme throughout the book, Soares has a lot of empathy for our natural preferences in this regard and others. We want to be lazy, amuse ourselves, and privilege our friends. We’re monkeys running on hardware that wasn’t meant to grapple with any of these questions.

Another place the principles-vs-gut tension comes out is where Soares grapples with expected value type thinking, and how we can derive that from some sense of what we “really” prefer. Here, he uses the thought experiment where ten identical unwitting copies of you are sent to ten different places where each one of them experiences the outcome of a positive expected value one-to-ten bet, where only one of the copies has to experience the negative outcome. Intuitively, when we think about the negative outcome befalling our singular self, it’s often so aversive that we refuse positive sum trades. But if you really imagined there being ten fully alive versions of yourself who would each live with the proportional consequences of the positive-expected-value bet, it’s easier to accept yourself being the one who drew the short straw.

That thought experiment in particular also made me reflect on suffering and how tolerant we should be of suffering in net-positive worlds. Where serious suffering is on the line, I notice myself having the same intuitive reaction as the singular-me version of the experiment—I get tunnel vision around the downside. The interesting question is whether I would personally accept some potentially extreme suffering if I had a visceral understanding of exactly who and how many people would benefit by how much from that suffering. I’m honestly unsure of the answer, or how much the non-identity problem resolves or doesn’t resolve this. The willingness I feel to endure a mildly negative life so that others could live in bliss suggests something about the possibility of a smooth curve (of some unknowable steepness) on which I should be making these trades. And it breaks down a little bit of my hard resistance against the idea that some suffering can be “justified.” Perhaps I should consider others just as strong and willing to sacrifice as I imagine myself being.

Rejecting badness of people

Another potentially non-identity-flavored theme in the middle of the book is whether or not it’s reasonable to say there are good and bad people. Soares channels the question through whether or not you should regard your goal in life as being a “good” or “bad” person, and reasonably answers no.
