You can think of your life as a series of actions and experiences, with each one being better or worse in terms of some concrete goal. Your goals can each be some combination of justifiable, compelling, and meritorious (or not). The question is not whether there are some objective goals, but just whether your particular goal is good, and whether continued effort towards improving those actions and experiences is justified by the cost of creating them in light of those goals. Perfectly sensible framing.

Still—and I think Soares might concede this subtly at some point—it makes sense socially to speak of good and bad people, at least for purposes of deciding who to trust, cooperate with, defect on, or otherwise respond to in view of their “goodness” or “badness.” It seems similarly reasonable to have “be trustable and loved by others” as one of your goals. While this isn’t necessarily identical with notions of being a “good person,” it rhymes enough for me to say it’s worth having the concept around. You can reflect on all you’ve done and place yourself on some continuum of people, and this will give you useful feedback on how well you’re doing as compared to some compelling goal we associate with “goodness,” even if we lack a precise definition.

Perhaps Soares would reject this framing as an example of the “good enough” type reasoning he lampooned at the top—you should be trying to optimize, not rest on your laurels once you’ve passed some arbitrary threshold! I mostly agree, but the feedback value of reflecting on what bars you’ve cleared means I wouldn’t put things as strongly as Soares did.

No one is evil and everything is broken

Finally, there’s Soares’s oft-repeated line “(almost) no one is evil, but everything is broken.” Perhaps per the good and bad person discussion above, the reason for saying no one is evil is just that it isn’t productive to think in those terms when you’re focused on marginal actions to make the world better. I’m happy to concede that “evil” is a stronger term than “not a good person” or even “bad person,” but I think this line sits a little bit uncomfortably with the book’s imperative towards fixing the world and reshaping the multiverse in the way that you want to see it. Sure, there are all kinds of coordination problems we could solve—indeed, you’re telling us to go out and solve them—but what should we make of the people who pay those problems no heed? Does Soares buy the act-omission distinction here? Or again, is evil just setting the bar a bit too high for those who in some sense choose not to build the better world we could have?

I’m tempted to open up this line of inquiry because I think trying to morally improve others is probably a fruitful direction for improving the world overall. Perhaps in Soares’s call to agency here, he rejects that. Perhaps he more confidently rejects it as a form of cope or pre-excuse (another theme in the book).1 I’m setting myself up to excuse my failure to fix the world by saying other people were evil and there was nothing I could do. That is not what I think I’m doing, but I suppose the possibility always lurks in the background.

Less cuttingly, Soares and I probably just agree that the way to make people reliably more moral is to reveal to them the parts of themselves that want a better world and to further help them realize that those parts are ones they want to nurture and strengthen.

1

I had another section called “Cynicism as cope” drafted, that was more of an aside:

One of the middle sections on toleration really spoke to my sense of how the well-educated deploy blanket cynicism. Discourse around Effective Altruism constantly turns this up. Some purported problems couldn’t be actual problems. Some interventions couldn’t possibly work. The former is frequently deployed on AI risk and biosecurity, but the latter can extend all the way to claims like bed nets being used for fishing as a reason to reject the urgency of distributing more of them.

This sounds too much like psychologizing the opposition. But when I see the reflexiveness of some of these takes from people who haven’t thought carefully about the problems at all, but assume they must either not exist or can’t be solved, I can’t help but feel from them some desperate resistance to the idea that if these problems are real or if these interventions worked, they would lack an excuse for helping work on them. I think we have enough critics in this genre such that some of them could be speaking to a genuine possibility we’re wrong, and that at least some others are definitely falling into this exact trap.

item.title: Transformative AI can only be Second-Species AI
item.description: Some perceived-by-me incongruities in models
item.content:encoded:
I’m confused about Seb Krier’s view here. Tyler Cowen shared it I think because it’s consistent with Tyler’s view of 0.5% extra GDP growth/year (enough to keep us at 2-3% for most of the century). But I don’t think that’s what Seb has thought, perhaps until now. I thought Seb thought the world will be radically transformed.

So my first question on reading this is whether Seb has changed his view on what the world of 2070 looks like. I thought he was in for Dyson swarms and mind uploads, but the claims in this tweet seem impossible to square with that.

I’ll stop talking about Seb now, I just wanted to anchor my more general remarks on a realer conversation being held by people who think more about AI than I do. My point here is the incongruity between the Dyson swarms and the systems-not-species view of AI.

That point is: You just don’t get a radically transformed world unless the AIs are calling the shots on a deep level. To do that, they have to be something like minds as distinct from tools.

A bunch of narrow AIs appended to human systems as-demanded by consumers seems like a likely outcome, but it’s not a transformative one. It’s incredibly bottlenecked by people being slow, asking the wrong questions, lacking vision, wanting the wrong kinds of solutions to fit their preconceptions, etc. When Tyler talks about University committees being a bottleneck to AGI sparking explosive growth, this is the world he has in mind. Some oracle-like, genius chatbot can give you some really good plan or idea for a new invention, but if it needs you to hold its vision in your head as you orchestrate other AIs and humans, that feedback loop just doesn’t allow for technological progress at the rate the TAI people talk about.

On the other hand, if the AI(s) can do everything unsupervised, without you in the loop (in principle at least, so we can make your managerial burden arbitrarily light and sidestep misalignment concerns), that just is another species/mind/organism—it’s acting fully autonomously towards a goal in the world. I may well be here because its inventor had particular goals in mind, but the whole misalignment discourse is then back in play. No one ever denied that AIs would face incentives of some kind; in fact, that was a big part of the worry.

If AIs are designed to fit human institutions and can accommodate humans in the loop, but don’t require them to function, a few people in a few places turn over everything to the AI and the AIs build whole new work streams and products from the ground up to rapidly outmaneuver competitors. Others copy this strategy (if the AIs don’t drive them out of business first), and we end up in a world fully and directly controlled by autonomous, agentic AIs.

I think what many people need is a few paragraphs describing what the full scope of “autonomous,” “agentic,” and maybe “everything” is. I don’t have it in me rushing this post out, but the amount of awareness, foresight, and creativity needed to do all economically useful tasks completely encompasses everything you need to be an independent mind. The possibilities of what the world could be like, and what your experience of it could be just have to occur to you if you’re able to do all the things to make it one way or another. The consequences of making it one way or another are even more obviously apparent. The idea that somehow a system that cares about driving some consequences but has to be strangely blind to others is either the whole misalignment problem distilled or incoherent.

Again, narrow tools integrated into human-centric workflows—even if quite agentic—just don’t get you that. They can make great suggestions, but if they need step by step approvals or have to be interpretable by their human principles (even on a shallow level), that’s too slow. Either we hew closely to those rules and get no economic explosion, or we throw them out and we get both an explosion and all the risk that comes with having the AIs in charge of everything.

A third possibility is that AIs are only ever capable of being narrow tools by default. Maybe you can have specialized “manager” AIs here too, but by hypothesis, they closely mimic their human principals and lack the breadth, creativity, and vision that a true AGI would have. This of course means no explosive growth and I think it is the only kind of AI thing Tyler is capable of imagining.

item.title: Reflections on NaBloWriMo
item.description: An exercise in shamelessness
item.content:encoded:
Writing a blog post every day this month1 has gone pretty badly. Here I’ll summarize some reasons why and then speculate on how to produce more useful stuff in the future.

This has gone badly

First, it felt like a burden. Maybe listening through Replacing Guilt halfway through and reviewing it was a sign. Every day, it was very apparent to me that publishing something was on my to-do list, which generally felt aversive and like it was constraining other things I wanted to do rather than the other way around.

Second, I didn’t plan. All I came in with were a few hundred short ideas I had jotted down in my notes app, with no more detail than could be captured in a couple sentences. Had I done some outlining or throwing in sources, or even written just twice as many sentences for each post, I might have had some more excitement around getting up and turning them into reality. That’s what I tried to do with my theses posts. But those posts themselves only came together during the month, so when any given day arose, I felt like the concepts I had distilled there were too important to rush out that day, given everything else I had going on.

Worst, I adjusted my expectations downward and felt more comfortable doing something akin to failing with abandon, namely, rushing out something near the 500 word mark in an hour or two with no willingness to change topic or even organization from the first thing that showed the barest beginnings of taking shape. Looking back, maybe things didn’t degenerate quite as quickly as I felt like they did. It wasn’t really until the 21st—ironically the day after the Replacing Guilt review—that I really started phoning it in. So there’s some chance I’ll end up believing that NaBloWriMo was a two-thirds success (more likely a half success).

What good writing looks like

Good writing needs to say what we’re all thinking. Readers have recurring thoughts and recurring frustrations around certain arguments and ideas. Good writing really distills these perspectives in a way where the reader is nodding along, saying, “Yes, yes, that is what I’ve been trying to put my finger on.” This also means that the thesis needs to be something difficult to put your finger on. Otherwise, it will just read as trite and obvious (though people often overestimate how high the bar for novelty is here). To do a good job distilling something like that, you have to at least have gone through the argument a number of times in your head, or probably with some other person who feels they have a stake in it. It’s hard to do that 30 times a month.

Good writing needs to bring out a common mistake. Relatedly, good writing also needs to come quite close to getting parties who disagree with the thesis to agree that you’re hitting on the crux and at least attempting to answer an accurate version of their objections. Without that, you’re not having the debate that matters, i.e. the one that’s actually happening or the one that feels like it has the power to potentially change views.

Most importantly, good writing needs to be infused with the spirit of a writer who knows what they’re saying is important. You need to care about what you’re writing. I have some sense of pride that needs to be vindicated in everything I publish, but pride alone is not enough and it doesn’t help that my expectations are (and have been) adjustable. The standard “pride at all” is a far cry from the feeling of investment I had in some posts whose subject matter felt acutely alive to me on the day of writing: FTX, Soul of EA, and 80k. No wonder they did well.

An audience’s enthusiasm for a piece of writing is best modeled as some (small) fraction of the author’s enthusiasm. If I as a writer am not bursting at the seams to get something through to my audience, chances are very few people will give the post their full attention, much less find real value in it.

Sadly for me, I only experience that fervor a few times a year. There may be ways to cultivate it, but daily obligations ain’t it.

1

My very online housemates have informed me that the “generic” term for what Inkhaven is is “NaBloWriMo”—national blog writing month.

item.title: Five Components of Taking Ideas Seriously
item.description: Which could probably be reduced to two
item.content:encoded:
In the course of drafting a plan to make Effective Altruism great again, I’m trying to pin down and decompose some central principles that make EA ideas and thinkers seem so vital. Perhaps chief among these is the notion of taking ideas seriously. Taking ideas seriously sounds all well and good, but what do we mean by that? As is my wont, I have narrowed down five things that I think serve as useful guides.

Willingness to go to weird places

This first principle speaks to how you orient to ideas as things distinct from just anything you happen to say or believe. Namely, ideas evoke something more abstract and principled. They’re the kind of thing you can expound upon and mix with your empirical experience of the world to produce new insights.

An important question then becomes how willing you are to accept those insights. If you’re taking ideas seriously, I claim, you need to be willing to accept ideas at least enough to continue considering the places they might take you.

For example, if you don’t let a principled concern for pleasure and pain extend to real consideration of the pleasure and pain experienced by insects, maybe you aren’t taking the idea that pleasure and pain are what’s important seriously.

Willingness to reject popular beliefs

This principle extends the first by letting you arrive at weird places over and above just going there. Should shrimp welfare be our priority? It’s a question you need to be able to ask, and if all the arguments point to yes, even in the face of other problems that humans are facing, you should be willing to stand by the arguments instead of saying “but that’d be crazy, right?”

Similarly, if a powerful argument leads you to think that the long-term future contains many more lives and morally higher stakes, you should be able to accept the conclusion that this is what many more people should work on despite the desperate situation that many people today face for certain.

The real move here is holding reductio arguments to the high bar of actually revealing an inconsistency or inherent contradiction in an idea, rather than dismissing it for being merely uncomfortable.

Willingness to debate

Willingness to debate is another extension of the general principle we’ve been hovering around, in this case applied to specific people, groups, or positions that polite society would excuse rejecting out of hand. This is just another easy excuse not to explore ideas and instead rely on customs or heuristics.

If an idea or a person shocks your conscience and triggers moral outrage, you should be able to explain why and—at least in principle—tolerate hearing and responding to the arguments, even if you don’t think it’s a great use of time.

Being calm, accessible, pedantic, and positive

The way to actually let yourself follow ideas where they lead in a practical sense is to control your own emotions. The three principles above each rely on notions of what is socially acceptable or unacceptable, i.e. weird. If you get past those and are willing to engage and potentially agree with any proposition, you still need to remain consistently calm and focused on using plain language and precise meanings. A general air of positivity probably helps here too.

The issue is that failing to embody these traits is strong evidence that you’ve let some non-argued-for factor take over. This is because ideas should be free-flowing and allowed to go whichever way the arguments point. You as the one pursuing ideas should be happy for them to do that.

Getting upset that ideas have failed to flow in a particular direction is a clear sign that you’re not fully committed to exploring them wherever they lead.

Tolerance of reasonable disagreements

Further internalizing things, you should be able to recognize—and indeed applaud—perspectives that are ‘good,’ and ‘very good,’ even if they do not match your own ‘best’ view. If you’ve personally explored ideas to the furthest extent you’re able and reached a stable conclusion, you should make an effort to understand reasonable grounds for disagreement based on unshared assumptions about the subject at hand. If you are unwilling to accept assumptions which aren’t yours, you likely underexamined the foundations (and fundamental uncertainty) of your own beliefs. This means it will be hard to unmoor you from any belief, including false ones.

item.title: Is This All a Doomed Enterprise?
item.description: Thinking in the limit might mean thinking about inevitability
item.content:encoded:
What I’m trying to do with AI is indirect. I want to alert people to the fact they’re coming up to this pivotal moment in history, and help them relate to the gravity of that. I don’t know what strategies and approaches will make sense in the wake of a broader appreciation of our circumstance, but I’m more open to what happens with broad appreciation than I am to what happens without it.

In that light, my question about whether we’re all doomed is not the traditional empirical one: “Will AIs displace and make obsolete flesh and blood humans?,” but a bigger picture framing on whether a good universe is even possible in the long run. Avoiding AI extinction this century wouldn’t amount to much in the scheme of things if it was just a tiny bump on the inevitable road to a bad universe. It might simply preserve our net-negative world for a few more decades before immutable forces of competition and selection land our descendants in an even worse world. It also might not, but this is the thing to figure out.

This is all a prompt for you to look at Joe Carlsmith’s “Can Goodness Compete?“ and a related podcast here.

The question presented there is whether the universe has some predictable ultimate end state based on the types of actors and incentives that get selected for, given enough time for them to emerge and compete, and whether that end state is good.

The problem within that is whether the universe invariably selects for power and the ability to occupy matter and space. If the answer is yes, it seems like “goodness,” as we conceive of it, might not have a place in the limit. This is because any resource dedicated to goodness—things like rest, beauty, or joy—is a resource that could have been dedicated to power, control, or expansion. If you have two systems starting out with equal resources, the one that invariably chooses power and growth will, in the fullness of time, eclipse any system that chooses to allocate even a few resources towards goodness (or indeed anything that’s not power-and-growth).

I’m of at least two minds about this. The crux is whether there is such a thing as “slack.” Slack is the resources left over after you’ve done everything you need to do to secure your position from maximally power-seeking competitors. This could look like a star system-wide benevolent government where interstellar conflict is physically unviable and every strategy for overthrowing the government from within is adequately prepared for. The key is that the costs of unassailable defense and security are not total: there are still resources left over to spend on good things. It’s not obvious that this would be the case. It’s a question of offense-defense balance at technological maturity. It could just be very cheap to destroy social stability as a technical matter, where no matter how much you invest in security, there will still be gaps for virus-like destructive forces to creep in and the only stable equilibrium is perpetual destruction and predation. Kill or be killed.

The hopeful story is that there are systems and strategies that allow powerful good-seeking entities to quash entities that might contest goodness very cheaply, quickly, and efficiently, so as not to tax all of their goodness away.

The less hopeful story is that power-seeking entities are so strongly selected for and incentivized that they’ll continue to emerge and evolve until the tax on goodness grows high enough that we end up in something we’d recognize as the kill-or-be-killed world.

While I don’t have an answer to the ultimate question, I do think it’s interesting to reflect on the fact that we know there is locally counterfactual good that we can do at large scales—at least in terms of what seems familiar to us now. You really can prevent hundreds of children from dying who would have otherwise died. You can also greatly improve conditions for hundreds of thousands, perhaps billions, of farmed animals who wouldn’t have had any respite but for your actions. I happen to think the world is net negative overall because of wild animal suffering, but we are still living in a non-Malthusian dream time where we each control more resources than we strictly need to preserve ourselves. We have options to create more good even if, like AI risk, this is just a tiny detour on the inevitable path elsewhere.

Whether you can extend what’s true on the margin in the dream time to the technological limit is the core question. The immediate choice we face is whether to trade away big-on-a-human-scale opportunities in pursuit of an uncertain, but potentially vastly good future.

item.title: America is Under Attack
item.description: Whether it's happening slow or fast doesn't matter
item.content:encoded:
There will be ICE agents at key polling sites in November. We know this because it would be beyond facile to think that the Trump administration’s cycle of escalation has some natural terminus that just happens to approximate the events of the last ten days. Do you honestly think that masked men disappearing people in the streets, renditioning legal residents to third world concentration camps, deploying soldiers to politically disfavored cities, redrawing maps to steal people’s votes from them, and brazenly lying to defend the murder of a soccer mom was all just a setup to bring interest rates down by a thousand basis points because it’s fun to watch numbers next to stock prices get bigger?

Of course you don’t think that. But you don’t want to form a specific view on where this ends either. You assume politics is a crowded field and surely many other people are taking the relevant precautions and shoring up the guardrails. Centrist Republicans, the Democrats, the courts, the news media.

I have bad news. Each of those groups is flailing and failing spectacularly right now. The first doesn’t exist anymore. Maybe 3% of Republicans had some attachment to principle and broke off from the demagogue train. All the others got on it. The Democrats see each new crisis as a cheap ticket not to change a thing and simply reap the 4-point bump in the polls that falls short of giving them the power to actually do anything. The Supreme Court is tip-toeing around enjoining brazen illegality in the self-defeating hope that this preserves the administration’s willingness to abide by their future orders. The news media can’t help but be led along like a cat chasing a laser pointer with each new scandal erasing any memory of past scandals in a matter of days. Further, they can’t be asked to exercise *any* editorial judgment, including basic use of the five senses and common English words. Every story is “something happened, Republicans say good, Democrats say bad, here they are in their own words.”

Looking back at what’s happened in the past year brings into relief everyone’s failure to think even one step ahead:

  1. Trump pardoned everyone who attacked the Capitol on January 6 and then rewrote the history of that day to vindicate a direct attempt to overthrow our elected government.

  2. He ordered that citizenship be denied to people born on US soil, a direct attack on the Constitution.

  3. He’s unleashed 20,000 largely untrained, unqualified, masked men in unmarked cars to roam American streets, assault and disappear people without warrants, probable cause, or evidence. Many citizens have been detained, several residents have died in custody, we’ve all been subjected to lawless violence on our streets.

  4. He’s violated court orders barring him from flying freshly-detained residents out of the country without charges or a hearing to put them beyond the reach of our laws. Likewise with orders to return those people to the United States.

  5. One of his goons murdered a mother in cold blood for objecting to this. The President and Vice President repeatedly, brazenly lied about evidence the public could see with their own eyes, calling her a terrorist.

  6. He deployed the military to cities in peacetime without the consent of the people.

  7. He has used personal loyalty to him as a litmus test for jobs and appointments. Federal contractors are required to denounce anti-Trump ideology and his woefully unqualified cabinet picks share only unblinking, unthinking loyalty to Trump the man in common.

  8. Likewise, he’s weaponized federal contracts against his enemies, barring whole law firms from doing business with the government if any part of the firm ever represented his political enemies, taxing the legal representation of anyone who criticizes him.

  9. He illegally halted congressional appropriations to foreign aid and domestic climate programs. Tens of thousands of the world’s poorest people died.

  10. He’s illegally withheld funds from universities where he’s unpopular and launched a campaign to violate the first amendment rights of student visa holders by rescinding visas for students saying things he doesn’t like.

  11. He’s stopped holding daily press briefings and revoked passes for major outlets (the Washington Post, CNN), replacing them with sycophantic morons from YouTube. He’s stripped funding from NPR, PBS, and scientific grants for climate research, labeling them “propaganda.”

  12. He ordered Republican states to redraw their congressional districts to disenfranchise Democrats and gain unrepresentative seats for loyalists in his party.

  13. He created TrumpCoin as a tool to accept bribes1 that have resulted in multiple pardons for drug and crypto criminals and further accepted bribes from illiberal states like Qatar, personally enriching himself by billions at the expense of the public.

  14. He illegally started a trade war with every country on earth because of his personal theories of good policy, crippling jobs growth in manufacturing, raising consumer prices, and destabilizing the world economy.

  15. He’s refused to release the Epstein files despite a Congressional subpoena, openly flouting the law and breaking his campaign promise.

  16. He invaded Venezuela and killed hundreds without congressional authorization, sometimes violating the laws of war even beyond that. He’s threatened to invade Greenland, the sovereign territory of a peaceful, democratic country.

  17. He illegally fired an independent FTC commissioner and brought fabricated charges against two members of the Federal Reserve Board for the purpose of directly controlling independent agencies that safeguard the US economy.

Draw the trend line. Trump is not leaving office. Or he’s going to pull some Putin-Medvedev scheme where a stand-in who swears to be following his orders steps in. This is under the assumption that his political opponents keep their voting rights long enough for these sorts of gimmicks to be necessary. We’ve watched other countries do this. Eventually the opposition candidates get arrested and the voting infrastructure gets taken over. Every accusation is a confession.

You say that sounds extreme. America? Turning into Russia? Seems unlikely. It’s not like that’s happened to a superpower before…

My challenge to you is to predict where this escalation stops and why. No other Fed governors will be indicted despite not going along with the interest rate scheme? Just because? This year’s elections will run smoothly and then two Democrat-majority houses have their votes respected by the administration, which putters along for two years and bows out gracefully? Specifically because that’s what they didn’t do last time?

My own prediction is like that of my friends who project the lines on AI capabilities charts forward: there’s no natural, predictable stopping point. By the time Trump dies, there’s a good chance his successors will have enough hard power—gerrymandered districts, paramilitary voter intimidation, and state-level control over vote counting—that they don’t need Trump’s cult of personality.

The more optimistic story is that things unfold like last time. Amped up voter intimidation and election denial isn’t enough to stop Democrats from taking back the White House in 2028. Of course the Republicans lie and claim fraud with abandon, but they walk away on January 20, 2029 and we pick up the pieces for four years.

At a minimum, I think you have to concede that Trump will try harder to defeat American democracy than he did in 2020. Remember that he wasn’t starting wars, defying court orders, or fabricating criminal charges against independent officers then. It’s plausible that he’ll move to arrest the Democratic nominee or president-elect in 2028. Perhaps his security forces will just lock the new administration out of federal buildings and accounts.

In that case, it will come down to the military to honor their oaths to the Constitution. That seems like a “maybe” at best. They know civil violence would be an indelible scar on American history. They might think, even in that dark hour, that there’s still some way to “muddle through,” only to spend the subsequent years being eroded away themselves.

Even if they have the resolve, the whole military may be unable to get on the same page and follow orders from the legal commander in chief. Then either outcome is tragic. All this against the backdrop where Trump is already making life difficult for honorable service members who care about the law to continue in their posts today.

Again: where is this going? Where does it end? These are the questions you have to answer if you want to justify ignoring this slow rolling attack on America.

If, like me, you don’t see a clear end to this, the imperative is to keep a level head at the same time you embrace the urgency. Unfortunately, this moment we’re having with Jerome Powell and Renee Good will pass like all the rest. Each moment like this has revealed some cracks in Trump’s dam, but people’s attention moves on too quickly to the next crisis or distraction. But we do know there will be a next crisis and it’s probably only weeks away. Now is the time to build infrastructure to respond effectively next time.

We need phone campaigns to moderate Republicans. Even if ICE will come in to save their seat in November, I don’t think they’re banking on that.

Also, just because the November election will be under assault doesn’t mean we can’t force good outcomes anyway. The vote counting systems still seem robust. We can get people to pound the pavement and register folks. Have them vote early and vote by mail. Physically protect ballot drop boxes.

Most importantly, we can find ways to communicate better. Just the facts, just the things that matter to voters. At scale. We manufactured a whole vibecession two years ago; we can get people to see the actual threat to their way of life in front of them now.

Finally don’t give into or even indulge your anger. So much has gone wrong. And it’s gone wrong in no small part due to deep moral failings. If our society were a group of 30 intimate friends, expressing fury would be a credible signal that we’ve been profoundly wronged. Americans are not intimate friends though. We don’t know each other well enough for that and we don’t understand our situation. We haven’t—and can’t—have pre-supposed trust across 300 million people such that when one of us is furious, the others take it seriously.

Our best disposition is calm and strength. Build trust by demonstrating understanding and articulating a plan. It’s a sad irony that that is a large part of how Trump has gotten as far as he has: evincing total detachment and lack of emotion in his false descriptions of America as a ruinous hellscape. He is turning it into that hellscape. As appalling and evil as that is, people don’t understand. What they’re looking for is someone to dispassionately (but perhaps simply, and engagingly) explain what’s going on. I’m sure I have fallen short here. America’s finest public servant did not fall short yesterday:

item.title: Effective Altruism Will Be Great Again
item.description: Sequence thinkers will be forgiven and rejoice
item.content:encoded:
In some fleeting moments lately, I catch glimpses of 2022—the year Effective Altruism’s ascent seemed unstoppable. Universally positive (if limited) press, big groups at top universities across the world, a young EA entrepreneur was the darling of the financial industry, the first EA running for Congress calling in enormous financial and personnel resources for his campaign. More than those public-facing facts though, was a feeling on the ground that if you had a good grip on things and a plausible idea, you would get funding, go to the Bay, and make it happen.

I actually regret how slow I was to see it at the time. You could just do things, and yes, that’s always been true, but at that time, you didn’t even have excuses. In my first year as an advisor at 80,000 Hours, I allowed people a lot of excuses. I think this came from some emphatically non-prophetic feeling of “this is too good to be true.”

And, of course, it was. But now we’re here again: buoyed by another darling startup whose founders are committed to giving away most of their wealth to things that will do the most good™. Some of the same risks are present too.1 The biggest difference though, is how EAs now conceive of themselves and their movement. FTX proudly brandished its heart-and-lightbulb in one of the most brazen acts of moral self-licensure in history. Anthropic hems and haws about their relationship to scope-sensitive do-gooding.

But the future belongs to those who mince words less. I would like my friends at Anthropic and my EAs across the board to win the future. And while I can’t predict the *whole* future, I do predict that Effective Altruism’s flag will fly high and proud in the next few years. New projects will launch, ambition will again be the coin of the realm, and no one will be able to deny the underlying reality that a community formed of a commitment to understanding and bettering the world at scale is the reason why. The only decision to be made is whether this will happen in spite of us or because of us.

The Retreat

The case for “in spite of” is probably straightforward to most readers of this blog. The dizzying heights we reached so quickly in the FTX era set us up for an even more disorienting fall. EA’s decline into mild disrepute is mostly a consequence of EAs themselves playing into that catastrophizing narrative and refusing to hit back at their critics out of shame. While I think this is basically correct, a more nuanced account reveals why we might struggle to meet the present ascent as well as we could.

The FTX collapse was not just a lightning bolt of humiliation that shocked EAs into shame, it also accelerated two pre-existing trends in the movement: the professionalization of EA and the growing consensus that addressing transformative AI dominated all other cause areas in expected value terms.

Professionalization entails a lot of things. For one, when you’re the tiny germ of a new idea in the head of a few undergrads in 2009, your movement is about you, your friends, and how your call to action can be made consistent with everyday life, i.e., try to be smart about how you donate 10-50% of your income. When you draw 11-figure funding and have shored up consensus about some seriously novel, globe-spanning neglected problems, you’ll need to create some institutions and build some alliances. Now, you’re no longer asking people to modify their normal lives in light of your weird ideas; you’re modifying your weird ideas to meet the expectations of their competent, would-be implementers. At a minimum, you’ll want some nice offices, salaries, and HR policies, but the urgency of drawing the best possible implementers means you also need to make it clear that the subject matter they work on is the only exotic requirement: no pledges, no veganism, no evidential decision theory.

The consensus on AI hardly needs elaboration, but I do think a neglected frame here is noticing that the consensus is a triumph of something akin to sequence thinking. You achieve your ultimate goal by succeeding at each logical step leading up to it, so you focus on whichever step is in front of you. Want to do the most good? Just work on the most important problem. Want to get more of that work done? Get more people to do it. More people do it when you don’t get bogged down in reasons and morals and world models.

These two trends complemented each other too. As consensus around AI risk grew, so did the opportunity to be more legible to professional types. We don’t have to start with your empathy for the homeless man on the street, do the shallow pond experiment, sell you on RCTs, raise the animal welfare question, and then talk about the numbers at stake in nuclear near-misses to get you bought in on AI risk if we just need you to balance our books. We’re an interest group like many others, we think this newfangled AI might be bad somehow and it’s a really hot topic right now. Interested in helping out? We pay all right for a nonprofit.

The asceticism, veganism, group houses, and polycules sat in uneasy tension with that pitch. There was also a reasonable thought that when you start with first-principles philosophy, it’s hard to avoid people forming opinions on all kinds of things and breaking off into still-associated subgroups who present at least some risk of reputational contagion. So quite sensibly, you diversify your approach and see how promising it looks to have a clean, professional, not-very-ideological, arguably-non-committal AI safety “field” as opposed to an EA “community.”

And I want to be clear that although this isn’t my cup of tea, it is an emphatically worthwhile experiment. Relying on everyone to come around to your idiosyncratic world view is not a strategy. Everyone is not going to just. At some point, you need to play nice with people who see things very differently than you and make them feel fully respected if you want to accomplish big things. Professionalism and legibility are fine ways to do that. The worry is that you elevate means over ends. In your rush to be pragmatic and accumulate respect and power in service of a better world, you neglected the better world part, banking on the notion that you locked that in ten years ago.

What Greatness Demands

My view is that a vision of a better world and the principles that cultivate it are really hard to pin down. They require almost all hands on deck all the time. For this, I am really glad that Forethought exists and that Will MacAskill—who will never escape the Effective Altruist label so long as he lives—is near the helm.

The issue is that while we were feeling out professionalization and AI uber alles, FTX happened and what was an experiment became the only lifeboat in a storm. Nearly all hands left the deck. Even Forethought is framed as an AI project, though I’m heartened that they draw so much from history and prioritize helping society do moral reflection.

My real issue is that EA in all its forms is still so small. MacAskill shouldn’t be near the helm. He and all the other members of the original EA student group should expect some edge from being around so long as the movement grew and from being selected for the ambition to make the movement happen at all, but the way we’ll know EA is really winning is when the Oxford crew is wholly eclipsed by a new generation of even more ambitious and clear-thinking altruists.

And we won’t find them if our exclusive offer is cushy, well-scoped research roles at buttoned-up think tanks. To lead this movement, to safeguard the future for our highest values, we need to ask people to own the whole outcome: understand things from first principles, build and articulate their own world models. Tell us we’re wrong. Compel us to see the greater good and find the better solutions to create a better world.

You can’t instruct people, or even hire them, to surpass you like that if you regard yourself as holding all the cards and doling out your specific wisdom on specific topics. And to be honest, we know that compute governance, scary demos, and RSPs (gulp) are all pretty weaksauce. Maybe these being the only tools we’ve dredged up is symptomatic of the fact that lots of people in this space can’t even articulate the central worry that well.

Perhaps there are no better ideas out there. We’re going with what we’ve got. Time is short. Understandable. My pitch is that we invest more in giving people the whole picture—from the beginning. Why are we here? What’s our best picture of the good world? How did *we* locate the problems we’re most worried about now?

When I ask the most admirable and impressive people trying to save the world at scale how they got into this line of work and what pushes them to the laudable (but so far insufficient) heights they’ve reached, the most common story is the classic EA one. “I wanted to do good; I wanted to understand how to do good.” They ran into Singer. They read old 80k. They spent time with the abstractions and debated Pascal’s Mugging. They found the best tools and they built their own models. Now they’re leaders who rely on those models and the judgment they gained building them to make a hundred decisions a day and steer their projects to value in a hostile and confusing world. Most of all, they believe in the tools more than the conclusions.

The best of us are all relatively heads-down on last mile projects though.2 This might be crunch time. In expectation, this is the most essential work. If no one is doing this and gaining traction, why would anyone feel compelled to sign on? The uneasy de-emphasis of Effective Altruism qua Effective Altruism is holding well enough and bringing EA fully back into the arena is several full-time jobs.

We’re still small. Retreating from FTX arguably made us smaller and less able to bounce back. The baseline reality is that great people still keep the good in their hearts though and despite their full plates they’re more and more willing to say so. It has always looked silly to deny it. And more than anything, there’s nothing here worth denying.

Effective Altruism is Good and Right

The point that I began to bleed into above is that sequence thinking can solve specific problems and make smart bets in context, but it doesn’t make strong people generally. Taking up the task to understand and act in the world does. That task is deeply personal and inherently open-ended. One’s orientation towards it should not be “what’s in the news lately?” or “how do I get a good job out of this?”

The orientation you want is: “what kind of person do I want to be?” I suspect that to even ask the question immediately pushes you towards some tentative answers. You want to do good. You want to help others. You want to be fair minded about that, maybe even impartial. You want to do more good rather than less. You want to believe true things and understand the world. To modern ears, it can sound cringe and over-earnest, but what other answer can you give?

And the reason EA will be great again is that the best EAs, of which there are many, all want to be EAs. It’s in their bones. If they weren’t staring down the barrel of an intelligence explosion, or if the prospect of transformative AI somehow disappears with relative certainty, they would open their Animal Welfare for Dummies books the next day. Or they’d roll up their sleeves to defend America. Some of them are doing these things now. The point is that the EAs are ready to do what’s right with no fuss and no ego. Believe it or not, that’s what AI safety work entailed just seven or eight years ago.

I know this because I know them. And to know them is to see the earnestness and care they put into understanding our situation and letting their views be guided by sturdy conceptions of the good, deep humility, and above all regard for what’s actually true rather than what sounds good. There’s a hunger for that in people: somewhere they can do real thinking about what really matters.

Values-agnostic arguments for AI risk surely have their place in the broad sweep of public discourse. And it may even be a big place, jockeying among all the other object-level, point-scoring rhetoric out there, but a large class of special people will always have an allergy to it. They want to understand how this fits in with everything else happening in the world, how this fits in with their highest ideals and what they want their lives to be about. The METR graphs just don’t offer that. Effective Altruism does.

1

Even though no one suspected fraud, people were worried about a crypto bubble in 2022, just as they’re worried about an AI bubble now. Also oh boy, first draft of this post was before the DoW snafu.

2

The reader will note that I am not the best of us.

item.title: If Anyone Bursts It, Effective Altruism Dies
item.description: FTX logic in the age of AI hype
item.content:encoded:
Contra my optimistic declarations of a few weeks ago, I concede that there are worlds where Effective Altruism does not recapture and surpass its past glory. Most of those worlds are ones where AI becomes a much less big deal in the world, or, more conservatively, fails to show signs of radically transforming the world in the next five years. EAs are writing bigger and bigger reputational checks here that reality might not cash. If those checks bounce, I worry EAs will struggle to recover the minimal social capital they need to make good things happen in the world generally.

The backdrop for this is the vast difference between the EA community’s investment in the transformative AI hypothesis and the rest of the world’s investment in it. Crucially, the rest of the world also has an opinion on AI and will take a victory lap if we turn out to be wrong (unlike bed nets or biosecurity, which they don’t think about). It’s true that the markets give some weight to the TAI hypothesis, but most of the world, most of the markets, and most of the experts put it at decidedly less-likely-than-not. Given how hard last-mile AI companies are hemorrhaging cash, their failure to turn some big corners soon may trigger a run for the exits and with that, a broad consensus that the AI-hypsters were wrong and foolish.

To be clear, I think that assessment will be unfair—given the information we have now, it makes eminent sense for society to do vastly more work preparing for potentially transformative AI. Unfair though it may be, this hypothetical judgment of foolishness does suggest a potential kind of meta-foolishness we’re engaging in right now. Namely, there might be very cheap, perhaps even costless ways to hedge our bets by demonstrating some self-awareness about what a disfavored, minority position we hold with respect to AI. It’s a hard thing to do when you’re a fast-growing minority with compelling arguments on your side, but let’s try anyway.

A Dialogue (2022)

SBF: Global utility is linear with respect to money, so I’m going to be perfectly risk neutral. The Kelly criterion strictly loses expected value compared to this.

Me: Wait, is it still linear over a marginal $26 billion?

SBF: Roughly yes, at least that seems more likely than not.

Me: Are you sure you’re perfectly calibrated on your risk neutrality? Like you might not be erring on the side of more risk than the expected value would dictate?

SBF: No more likely than I’m being too risk averse.

Me: Any thought to the externalities to the EA brand and to every other tech billionaire who might be put off by Big Good if things go south?

SBF: Oh, so we should stop doing EA to protect EA? I thought this was about the global poor and animals and future generations... excuse me.

*FTX crashes.*

EA: That was very bad. We denounce reckless risk taking, ignoring side constraints, and refusing to hedge or defer to industry norms.

EA, two months later: Interventions that assume TAI is coming soon strictly dominate interventions that do not assume that. Other approaches simply lose expected value compared to this.

— — —

Leading EAs are increasingly acting on the assumption that transformative AI will arrive within 5-10 years and that we’ll live through experience an intelligence explosion. While CoGi continues funding diverse conventional work on global health and animal welfare, the discourse has clearly made this turn. Most EA community builders have moved to values-agnostic “AI Safety field building.” Will MacAskill says that rather than the traditional 3 EA cause areas, we should have 16, 11 of which assume transformative AI is on the horizon. The 80,000 Hours Career Guide has been redrafted on the same assumptions (pre-order here).

As the dialogue above suggests, the basic tension is whether one should always do the EV-maximizing thing, even when it entails stark downsides for many of the worlds you’re quite likely to end up living in. I think SBF’s risk attitude with FTX was stupid, even on its own terms. For quite little money and opportunity cost, he could have hedged and secured his company’s long-run financial position. But instead of spending that money, or holding back on those speculative investments (which he also broke the law to make), Sam tried to max EV by his own lights and landed us all in a world where EA, AI safety, animal welfare, and global health are all poorer and less reputable to an extent we would have gladly given up a few billion dollars in 2022 to avoid.

I know EA does not exist for the sake of the EA community itself, but I think the abstract-principles-first community—and the specific individuals making TAI predictions presently—are valuable enough to consider whether there are cheap hedges against the fallout of being fundamentally wrong on AI as well.

Some Reasons AI Might Be a Bubble

To set the stage for why we should do more hedging here, it’s worth gesturing at what the rest of the world is thinking. As Rob Wiblin aptly put it: most people look at what AI can do today; people worried about transformative AI are looking at the delta between what I can do today and what it could do yesterday. When it comes to forecasting the future, the delta seems like the more useful thing to look at and extrapolate. The counterpoint is that all trends continue right up until they don’t.

It’s true that so far the trend-extrapolaters have been mopping the floor with people calling the top, but one need only look at the empty night sky in our 14 billion year old universe to wonder if this process has a natural ceiling somewhere well short of superintelligence. Indeed, we’ve already canceled the singularity once. At bottom, the question is: which capabilities does an intelligence explosion require and how far are we from those. Conceding that we’re getting directionally closer all the time, it’s still reasonable to call it a long way between here and there.

For example, writing—the one thing LLMs should be best at—is still a real weak point. Opus 4.6 added nothing to this post in its couple of attempts to fill in an outline I made, failing to be noticeably better than any of its predecessors. It focused on having a generic, over-confident, pseudo-profound blogger voice despite having 15,000 words of context from my best blogs, and it also missed some logical points like the difference between EV and raw likelihood in some of the hammy sentences it inserted throughout the post.1 Further—and I’m sorry to be such a wordcel here—you have to concede that Gemini in your gmail client is basically a terrorist and turning it off in various G-Suite apps is becoming a part time job for many of us.

A commonality across these and other AI under-performances is that AI tools basically never understand the nuance of “what you want” or what would be good in the context unless you spell it out in painstaking detail or really don’t care and any old approximation of a task will do. The former has always been true of AI and persists despite many predictions it would fall away very soon. The latter predicts AI will be useful only on the lowest-value parts of knowledge work, and that’s far less than a harbinger of dyson spheres in the 2030s.

Contrast these skeptical priors with how much of the argument for TAI-soon is grounded in deference to people at labs or otherwise CS-pilled folks. They aren’t the most relevant experts, but are often among the most biased ones—it’s their field making these objectively impressive breakthroughs and often being under-appreciated for it. It’s also their friends who are seeing their net worths climb into ten figures.

The deference to AI-makers in particular seems especially misplaced when you consider that the explicit analysis they’re giving us does not turn on their technical knowledge. They simply note that the models keep getting better and it doesn’t feel especially hard to make them better, i.e. the same trend extrapolation anyone else can do. They don’t tell us where ceilings might or might not lie beyond registering a prediction that “things will start to feel really hard before they stop completely, and they don’t feel really hard yet.” That’s something, but it’s not a guarantee and this class of people have been talking a very big game for over three years about what’s coming next amid progress that has been steady, but less than mind-blowing.

Ultimately, it’s reasonable for people to set the bar for full human substitution extremely high and to doubt that data on the internet captures everything that needs doing with enough fidelity to jumpstart an intelligence explosion. Ultimately, the specific, concrete drivers of value creation/innovation/transformation are just quite mysterious. The market does its still-quite-noisy best to reward the inputs that matter, but we really don’t have a gears-level understanding of how humans design and distribute world-transforming technologies. Without that, we can’t confidently say today’s models are proceeding orderly towards those abilities.

Pascal’s Ratchet

If I get into it with people about the content of the previous section (which I almost certainly will), I expect to feel like the burden of proof will be on me. That’s partly for bullshit social reasons because our tribe is AI-pilled and my interlocutors will feel the wind at their back, but it will also reflect the stakes of transformative AI. It is the ultimate ‘big if true’ claim about the world. The claim remains extremely big if there’s only a small chance that it’s true. If you’re anywhere over 10% on an intelligence explosion in five years, there’s not really an argument that anything else is of comparable importance, so I better be damn sure before I go talking people out of focusing on this.

Contrast this with how often Pascal’s mugging came up in the early days of AI risk discourse: should we invest everything to confront tiny, but non-zero chances of unfathomable loss where the numbers say that’s the highest EV thing to do? Usually, Pascal’s mugging was invoked as a reason not to work on things like AI risk. The probabilities were just too small, the reasoning went, and you can’t let tiny numbers multiplied by astronomically large stakes dictate your life. The chance that this is noise emanating from a true value of zero is too high and the pragmatist in us should prevail in cases like these.

At some point in the early 2010s—perhaps before—people in EA circles decided the odds were not so Pascalian. The probability of transformative AI this century climbed into the range where it clearly warranted serious investment and attention. I think they were (and are) right.

But since then, I fear a sort of powerful motivated reasoning kicked in. We know we’re above the threshold where we’re no longer being Pascal’s mugged, and any minor negative update we get doesn’t push us back below that threshold. But, since the vast majority of the world doesn’t realize the precarious situation we’re in, every positive update that we are in the TAI world is vital evidence to help people “wake up.” So negative updates get dismissed as not-decision-relevant, and positive updates become the currency of progress. This produces a subjective sense that AI is ratcheting up to ever more undeniable importance.

To be patronizing about it, this is a very epistemically comfortable place to be. You have good arguments. You’re confident (enough) in them. *Your* meta-rationality does not require you to change focus or even question your basic assumptions and the world just keeps feeding you (useful! important!) confirmatory evidence. The arguments are clever and neglected too. Physicalism, the Jones model, Bio-anchors, benchmarks. You can illuminate discussions and win arguments with these all day. My concern is that you’ve stopped meeting people where they are or dismissed them altogether because they’ve failed to “get it” despite what feels like (to you) overwhelming evidence.2

Cheap Hedges

It’s worth emphasizing that most of the “consensus” around AI risk is born of deference: sometimes to specific people, but oftentimes just to the vibe within the EA community, i.e., most people pushing the TAI-soon line actually don’t have their own independent grip on the Jones model, etc. The move is to anchor on one or two pieces of evidence you’ve heard—usually some version of the METR graph (which METR keeps telling you you’re misusing and overweighting!)—and then do Pascal’s Ratchet. And that actually works for a naïve EV-maximizer. My claim is just that we should aspire to be more than naïve EV-maximizers.

Look, of all the things in the world to maximize, I’ve got to admit, EV is a great one. Especially where the V is total welfare. Some of my best experiences have been welfare-dense ones. I want that to be more likely for more people. Some kind of Bayesian subjective-probability-weighted approach also seems like a good way to make sense of my options and obstacles here.

The problem for me is that I pretty deeply don’t trust myself, even on the Bayesianism-seems-better point, you may be terrified to learn. My gut kind of screams at me that propositions about the future always resolve 0 or 1 and the reasons I can access beforehand may just be a tiny, tiny fraction of all reason-space there. So I can weigh my evidence and place my bets, but I’m going to live in one of those objectively 0 or 1 worlds. The trouble is, when I reflect on how strong my reasons are, those TAI-0 worlds seem like a lot of worlds. I agree they have less value in them, but they could be, you know, real.

My undergrad response paper on Pascal’s Wager highlighted the risk of wasting 100% of your life worshiping a God you didn’t believe in. Yes, that 100% was infinitesimally smaller than the hypothetical eternity in worlds where God was real, but if you ended up not in those worlds, it turns out that the biggest actual value was just your life. And you had wasted it. All of it—your only chance to ever be, experience, or change the way things were. That was where the largest, most important value was, by far, in the actual world, and you ignored it for a hypothetically larger one. It made sense ex ante, but ex post, you were ruined for it.

And perhaps it is worth risking ruin for EA here. You’d get no complaints from a straightforward EV analysis. All you really lose is the ability to lean on this explicit ITN framing and the network built around it. While some of the bigger figures might have to keep their heads down on future matters of large public concern,3 all the people in EA could move on to other valuable projects with the only loss being this nice coordination mechanism for finding your people.

At the end of the day, dramatic bets on things most people dismiss are the most acute points of leverage in the world, they might even be the engine that turns history. So we have to bet, and we should bet big on AI. But one quality of that bet has been a visceral, stubborn insularity and denial about how much the world at large disagrees with us and why. “Look at the CAIS letter, look at the METR graph. How could you deny we’re on the precipice of something huge?” The problem is that I can just as easily say “look at the bond markets and look at the academic literature. How can you deny this is speculative?”

I think deep humility is a free lunch we’re ignoring here. There’s lots of evidence that there are many worlds where we’re wrong. We could work on acknowledging that evidence and articulating those worlds. We’re prioritizing AI most fundamentally because we have some philosophical priors about the nature of intelligence and, when we weigh those up against bio-anchors and AI investment growth, it adds up to a plausible story. Being clearer about that rationale—the real rationale that’s not METR graphs or deference to not-so-impartial CS-heads—might make us more compelling. Demonstrating our ability to understand and value problems in the world that make more sense to others is also a good way to demonstrate credibility and build coalitions about addressing AI risks among people with different or absent priors on these matters.

I’ll Still Be Here

I warmed up to the TAI hypothesis because people who demonstrated their knowledge of and concern for smart interventions on animal welfare, global health, and economic growth seemed to care a lot about it. In some ways, I was trapped in my neartermist, EA-libertarian world and someone reached down into it to pull me out. I worry we aren’t doing that reaching-down anymore and it might be fairly cheap to do—not just as AI safety advocates, but as well-rounded people who want a better world and who try hard to create it. I’m very grateful to my funders and supporters as I embark on doing my bit here and hope that my heavily-AI-pilled friends see me and my project as a valuable one by their own lights.4

Those AI-pilled friends of mine are the best we scope-sensitive do-gooders have to offer. This is why I worry so much that a legible bursting of an AI bubble will, as a sociological matter, tank their credibility—credibility that, if preserved, would have enormous value in the non-TAI future.

So I hope that, conditional on the AI bubble bursting, I’m wrong about the social consequences for these folks. And I’ll commit here and now to defending their decision to go hard on AI risk given the information we had at the time. I’ll leave only modest criticism about their excessive risk appetite, deference cascades, and neglect of pluralism. That sounds like a lot, but these are all things we can correct and I’m happy to be getting started on correcting them now.

One potential source of bias for me here is that so many otherwise interesting people I know have become these flat, one-dimensional “what about AI tho:” types. Why can’t we all be more like Daniel.

Cullen helpfully pointed out that typically pundits actually catch disproportionately little shit for failed predictions, so my appeal to consequences may be weaker than my appeal to people’s desire for a high-trust and highly-trustable core community of a few thousand people. Those people would worry a lot more about how much attention and dedication they should give the ideas that emanate from EA. Second and third impressions of people like this might matter more than the general public’s first impressions.

It’s arrogant to say, but I think I’m good at making the case for EA and I want to go out there and reproduce myself (and hopefully be the seed for EA communicators to surpass me!).

item.title: All The Pasts I Can Never Go Back To
item.description: She softened hard hearts
item.content:encoded:
It usually takes about six months for me to miss a place. I lived in DC last summer, nominally in a dusty row house room I rented off of facebook marketplace, but I spent virtually all my time at the wework a half-hour walk away where my friends would come in to work their 9-5s. It was the hottest summer in DC in a while, so the 30 minute walk there was often rough, even late and early. The contrast between the deep, hot, humid air outside and the frankly excessive A/C gave me a sensation like the one you get from a sauna and ice bath.

It was rough going. I wasn’t crazy about my job and I didn’t really enjoy much meaningful social time outside of some nice run-ins at the office. I tried playing Breath of the Wild in the living room at the row house, but the TV there started crashing so frequently that it became unviable. I took a day off to try and find an accessible soccer field with goals I could shoot at, and struck out at all four candidate locations I dragged myself through the heat to find.

Berkeley is way nicer—I’ve set up my room to be completely comfortable (and in my opinion beautiful); I love my housemates and my village; the weather is temperate; I’m sleeping better than I have in a long time and I really set my own schedule and priorities more so than I have since summer breaks in high school.

Still, I want to relive last summer in DC. My heart longs for London even more—that place that is so incredible to walk around by myself, but where I never felt more socially isolated. DC is a feeling on the roof of my mouth where the receding heat meets the deeper musical notes of the BotW soundtrack. London I actually feel in my chest cavity. Like loss.

That slightly sinking feeling is the one I have for Taerin and Gloria, deep relationships I could never relax in and commit to. My life as a lawyer in the dead center of downtown Chicago with my three-block commute and high-stakes (but charmed) firm job is an airy feeling in the back of my head. Law school lives in my shoulders. It was a little easier to relax them back then as I looked out the window from the best seat in the quiet-talking area of the library that I would seize for myself every morning at 8:30, including (and especially) on weekends.

Times before law school get fuzzier. I know I commuted by car (and sometimes regional rail) up to the suburban industrial park where I worked. There was also the long and messy saga of getting disentangled from my college girlfriend. There was the numbness and disorientation of losing my mom. It’s strange how steadily the waves of grief have gotten further apart, but they still come, 12 years later, now about twelve months apart. That period I feel in my throat and in my sinus and in my tear ducts.

At the very beginning of that period—when I still should have been in undergrad if not for a rush to graduate and move to New Zealand with my silver1—we got Delia. Well, I got Delia. After my sister and I failed in our venture to pick up 1-3 gray kittens we saw online the previous year, I was tempted to adopt a dog, inspired by my friend Martha who had just done that a year or two before. Mom had some criteria: no shedding and no barking, but otherwise my parents were very permissive about the whole affair despite their personal skepticism.

I don’t know how much I was intentionally fudging or self-deceiving when I settled on pit bull as the breed I wanted to go for. The fact sheet said mild-to-moderate shedding, a claim that was mildly-to-moderately undercut by the sparse, but consistent spread of short dark brown hairs covering the softer surfaces of our house a few months later. It was also the breed of Martha’s dog, Abel, who charmed me with his energy and range of facial expression.

I perused some rescue sites, and was taken aback by how much prettier one dog was than basically all the rest. Thinking back to our experience with the kittens, I assumed she’d have been taken or at least would be by the time we slow-and-deliberate Reardons would make a decision.

That wasn’t the case. My sister and I made a first visit at a shelter where Delia was bouncing off the walls. We took her out for a short walk around the block and she pulled on the leash so hard she sent me tumbling on the February ice just a minute out the door. We came back in and she peed on one of the dog beds in front of us, impatient to start sprinting around the room again. Katie thought Mom and Dad wouldn’t be thrilled about this dog behaviorally, but we should do it anyway.

Delia’s rescuer was patient with us and brought her over for a house visit before we committed. Dad was worried about liability. Mom was worried what the neighbors would think about us having a “pit bull.” Again, my parents proved a credit to liberalism.2 Delia came home to us on March 6, 2013, the birthday of our nanny, Czesia, who may have done half the work raising me and my sisters to high school age.

When Delia first came to us, I followed some generic advice about crate training that left her crying through many of her first nights. I can’t remember how long we stuck with it, but it broke our hearts and turned out to be unnecessary. Delia’s gentle demeanor and sense of dignity (occasional zoomies excepted) meant there was no danger to the furniture. She also made it easy to keep at least half my promise to Mom because she wasn’t much of a barker and took the hint that it wasn’t necessary from just a few hits of a (water-only) spray bottle.

The main challenge she posed for us was how to dispose of her excess energy. Thankfully, she never tired of chasing tennis balls. There was a spot you could stand up against the gate to our driveway where, with a little skill, you could throw the ball into the walkway along the side of the garage that went all the way back to the alley. Sprinting back and forth down that 100 foot path on the hard bricks—and putting the brakes on at both ends—probably contributed to Delia’s arthritis later in life, but it was what she lived for. Doing the same on the grass at the park a few blocks away was even better.

2013 was the year Mom was in remission. I’m glad she had Delia in the last year of her life. I can still picture her long fingers scratching Delia’s side and I remember how much Mom appreciated having someone to vent to who wouldn’t ask probing questions, insist on trying to fix things, or otherwise be difficult like her human children and husband. Dad felt the same way. I can’t remember if it was Mom talking about Dad or Dad talking about Mom when they told me it was “the best decision they ever made” to let me bring her home. In a moment of calm heading to the parking lot in the hour after Mom died, Emily said “thank God we have D,” thinking of Dad.

2015 is when Delia became Kevin’s dog. I went off to law school. He was very proud and I don’t doubt very glad for the company in his newfound empty nest. There’s a lot to be said for the structure of daily walks and the feeling of being needed. In general, Dad and Delia got along famously. Delia kept enough of the discipline I instilled in her in her first few months with us that she never took Dad’s largesse with people food as a sign she could tear the house apart or escape the yard as I’m sure Dad would have otherwise let her do.

I would come home for a week every few months and over the summers and get to enjoy some time with D and give her proper workouts in the park. She needed (or at least highly valued) those trips into her old age. We kept the same cadence when I moved downtown.

She was in Florida with Dad for most of the year when I moved back home during the pandemic, but we got the summer of 2021 together before I moved to London. She came in the car with us to the airport and I was really worried I wouldn’t see her again, being so far away and unlikely to come back often. I told her to be good, keep herself alive, and that I loved her.

It turns out D had a longevity streak in her. I wonder if it was the somewhat intense research I did on dog food brands when we first got her. Probably not. She and Dad continued going back and forth from Chicago to Sarasota every year up until this one. I got to see her in Chicago after I came to stay with my dad and stepmom after I quit my job in September-October of 2025. I had been surprised she could still chase the tennis ball in the park in 2024, but that was no longer the case. She was still able to muster almost as much excitement at the prospect of a walk or people food as before, but her days of dragging people along the sidewalks and living room zoomies were over.

She and Dad made one last trip down to Florida this winter. My sisters reported back from their visits in January and March that Delia looked pretty bad. Not moving much, struggling to get up and down from short couches, and later, not keeping food down and losing weight. I called Dad, worried that he’d be too married to habit and a desire to deliberate rather than do what was necessary to reduce Delia’s suffering and end our time together on a good note instead of one clouded by pain. I was right to worry. “The vet said it’s not time yet.” Of course, that vet visit was a month ago now, when she was still keeping food down consistently. I didn’t push too hard, but I let him know I would fly in and be there when the time came. I hoped he would take it as a sign to confront reality, if there was a reality to be confronted.

We spoke again a few days later and I made a plan to come down in two weeks. A few days after that, Dad texted me saying “it may be the right time to come down (now).” I was on a plane four hours later.

I got to spend one and a half days with her before the end. She was skinny and lethargic, but seemed tense and had trouble sleeping for long bouts even though she had no energy and could barely move. Twice on the day she died and twice on the day before, she picked herself up and made it to the corner of the patio where she could go potty—the expression I used years before when I’d show her two empty hands as I opened the kitchen door to convey that I wouldn’t be following her out to play. Her heart was pounding on those patio walks and I had to pick her up from two falls. She didn’t like being picked up. She’d tense up even more. Stress to add to the pain. I tried to tell her she could just go inside. The old rules were over now. She just needed to be comfortable.

She would give in to my pleading to take food or water only after I made at least three efforts. This and her brief moments of lucidity and eye contact were my only real signs that maybe she remembered me, maybe she was still here. I liked to think she waited for me, calling back to my sporadic visits of recent years. That’s my own indulgence though. We probably waited too long.

I expected the moment of putting her down to be the most painful thing I’d ever experienced, but almost all the grief came before. Imagining that moment, counting down the hours with her, apologizing for making her wait; praising her for hanging on so she didn’t die in the midst of some terrible seizure. When it did happen though, it happened fast. Maybe I was less present because I couldn’t sleep and there was a stranger in the room, but I stared into her eyes and said the things I wanted her to understand, mostly gently, but sometimes desperately: “You made it D, everything is going to be okay, you did such a good job taking care of us, we love you we love you we love you.”

I said the same things to my mom in the room where she died 12 years before. Mom was probably no more able than Delia to grasp those exact words in those final seconds of her life. Both of them were probably already gone in the sense that mattered when I said them. At least when humans get sick and admitted to the hospital they know what’s happening to them and what the range of possible outcomes are. There’s a mutual understanding between the dying and the people they leave behind that this is part of the deal, something they’ve all thought about and something from which they know there’s an imperative to move on and build lives.

Not so with dogs. It feels like we spend our whole lives with them trying to help them feel what we know. Things about love and preciousness without all the cognitive baggage of how things work and our hopes about how life goes after we lose people. Humans know about moving on. Dogs don’t. Grief is the price we pay for love. And a dog’s love is so unmediated by knowledge and intellect—things that so often serve to temper emotion—that the grief hits harder. Some part of me was trying desperately, futilely, to tell Delia “understand what’s happening so you can cope and take the edge off of it.” But all she felt was pain, and love, and then nothing.

She’s another one of my pasts now. One that spanned the last of my formative years, my first romantic love, my first real job, the first time I really left home, saying goodbye to my mom, finding my people, then pursuing what matters to me.

I could go back to DC and walk the same route, go back to the same office, and look up at that same row house. I’ve already done this in London, and Boston, and Chicago. Parts of it fill me up, make me smile. I recognize them. They are now what they were to me then. But those are the thin parts. The façades of buildings and the names of streets. They aren’t who I was then and they aren’t the people I loved and the way I loved them then. Those I can never get back, not the way these feelings in my mouth and chest and throat want to have them back. I am not the same. I’m older and time moves faster. So, so fast. All I can do is create my here and now. Turn to life’s preciousness in hope that I’ll wish I could come back to this past too.
